body: Afghanistan’s current de facto flag is plain white with the black Arabic shahada, «لا إله إلا الله محمد رسول الله», centered on it. Kabul sits in a mountain basin: pale concrete buildings, shop signs in Dari and Pashto, crowded streets and dusty hills rising behind them. Beyond the cities are steep brown ranges, irrigated green valleys and flat-roofed mud-brick homes. Dry air makes distant ridges look sharp in bright sun; footsteps scrape on gravel, while traffic and market voices fill city streets. Clothing varies, including loose tunics and trousers, shawls, headscarves and modern jackets. People may greet one another with «سلام علیکم» or Pashto «ستړی مه شې» and address someone as «آقا» or «خانم».

Albania’s flag is solid red with a black, two-headed eagle centered on it, its wings spread wide. Tirana has pale apartment blocks, glass-fronted newer buildings, cafés and broad paved squares; elsewhere, steep mountains frame stone villages and the Adriatic and Ionian coasts have clear blue water. Sunlight strikes white walls hard in summer, while winter clouds settle low around the peaks. On streets, cars roll over patched asphalt and café cups clink beneath conversation. People wear contemporary European clothes, with lighter layers on the coast and coats in the mountains. Common greetings include “Përshëndetje” and “Mirëdita”; polite forms of address are “zotëri” and “zonjë”.

Algeria’s flag has equal vertical green and white halves, green at the hoist, with a red crescent opening toward a red five-pointed star at the center. Algiers rises in tiers above the Mediterranean: white façades, balconies, hillside roads and the dense, narrow lanes of the Casbah. Inland, the Atlas Mountains give way to vast Saharan sand and rock. Coastal daylight can be hazy; desert light casts short, hard shadows at noon. Traffic hums along seafront roads, and voices carry through markets. Dress ranges from jeans and shirts to headscarves, djellabas and traditional outfits. People say «السلام عليكم» or «واش راك؟» and may address a friend as «خويا» or «ختي».

Andorra’s flag has three vertical stripes, blue, yellow and red from hoist to fly, with its detailed coat of arms centered on the yellow stripe. The shield shows a mitre and crozier, red vertical bars, red cows and the motto “Virtus Unita Fortior.” Andorra la Vella sits in a narrow Pyrenean valley with stone-and-glass buildings, sloping roofs, shops and steep roads. Forested mountains turn green in summer and snowy in winter; low winter sun leaves streets shaded while ridges remain bright. Footsteps echo on stone, with traffic audible in the valley. People wear practical mountain layers or everyday urban clothes. In Catalan, greetings include “Bon dia” and “Hola”; polite address is “senyor” or “senyora”.

Angola’s flag has a red upper half and black lower half. At the center is a yellow emblem: a half gear crossed by a machete, with a five-pointed star above. Luanda’s waterfront pairs high-rises and broad roads with older pastel buildings and busy neighborhoods; Atlantic surf breaks along the coast. Inland landscapes range from green highlands to drier southern plains. Humid coastal light softens building edges, and rain darkens pavement in the wet season. Engines, street conversation and waves make distinct layers of sound. People commonly wear shirts, dresses, business clothes or bright patterned fabrics. Portuguese greetings include “Bom dia” and “Olá”; respectful forms of address are “senhor” and “senhora”.

Antigua and Barbuda’s flag has red outer sections framing a central downward-pointing shape: black at the top with a rising yellow sun, a blue band beneath it and white below. St. John’s has low, colorful buildings, the twin towers of its cathedral and a working harbor. Around the islands are pale beaches, turquoise shallows, mangroves and dry green hills. Strong tropical sun makes sea reflections shimmer; rain showers briefly deepen the colors of roads and roofs. Waves slap against boats and trade winds rustle palms. People wear lightweight everyday clothes, with beachwear near the shore. Greetings are in English, including “Good morning” and “How you doing?”; “sir” and “ma’am” are polite forms of address.

Argentina’s flag has three equal horizontal stripes, light blue, white and light blue, with a golden Sun of May bearing a face at the center of the white stripe. Buenos Aires has wide avenues, ornate stone façades, apartment balconies and the Obelisco rising above traffic. Farther out are flat Pampas grasslands, the Andes and Patagonia’s windy plains. Afternoon sun warms pale buildings; southern winds tug at coats and make flags snap sharply. Buses hiss at stops and café conversation spills onto sidewalks. Clothing is mostly contemporary urban wear, with practical layers in colder regions. People greet one another with “Hola, ¿cómo estás?”; “che” is familiar address, while “señor” and “señora” are polite.

Armenia’s flag has three equal horizontal stripes: red on top, blue in the middle and orange below. Yerevan’s broad avenues and squares feature pink and warm-gray volcanic-stone buildings; Mount Ararat is often visible beyond the city, across the border. Elsewhere are rocky highlands, deep gorges and stone churches set against mountain slopes. Clear sunlight picks out the texture of tuff blocks, while winters bring snow and muted skies. Fountain water, footsteps and passing cars sound through central squares. People generally wear contemporary clothes, adding heavy coats in winter. A polite Armenian greeting is «Բարև ձեզ»; respectful forms of address include «պարոն» for a man and «տիկին» for a woman.

Australia’s flag is dark blue, with the Union Jack in the upper hoist corner, a large white seven-pointed Commonwealth Star below it, and five white Southern Cross stars on the right: four seven-pointed and one five-pointed. Sydney’s harbour has the white, shell-shaped Opera House and steel arch of the Harbour Bridge; inland, red earth, low scrub and eucalyptus trees stretch beneath a wide sky. Light is often strong, though climates vary greatly. People commonly wear casual shirts, shorts or workwear, with jackets in cooler cities. Waves hiss along beaches, and cockatoos call sharply. A casual greeting is “G’day”; “mate” is a familiar form of address.

Austria’s flag has three equal horizontal bands: red, white, red, without an emblem. Vienna streets frame pale stone façades, tram wires and the tall Gothic spire of St. Stephen’s Cathedral; beyond the cities, steep green valleys rise into rocky, snow-capped Alps. Winter light is low and cool, while summer sunlight brightens café terraces. Trams roll with a metallic hum, and church bells carry across squares. People wear everyday European clothes, adding heavy coats, scarves and boots in winter; traditional dress appears at some regional celebrations. “Guten Tag” is a polite greeting; “Grüß Gott” is also common. Address unfamiliar adults with formal “Sie”.

Azerbaijan’s flag has equal horizontal blue, red and green bands, with a white crescent and eight-pointed star centred on the red band. In Baku, the curved glass Flame Towers rise behind pale limestone streets and the older stone walls of İçərişəhər. The Caspian waterfront is broad and windy; farther inland are dry plains and mountain villages beneath snowy peaks. Sunlight catches dust and cream-coloured masonry, while sea wind rattles loose fabric and traffic hums along boulevards. People wear contemporary jackets, shirts and dresses, with warmer layers in the mountains. “Salam” means hello; “Necəsiniz?” asks how someone is. Polite forms of address include “bəy” and “xanım”.

The Bahamas flag has three equal horizontal bands of aquamarine, gold and aquamarine, with a black triangle extending from the hoist into the bands. Around Nassau, low pastel-painted buildings, balconies and palm trees sit beside bright roads and a busy harbour. Offshore, shallow turquoise water turns deep blue beyond pale sand and coral shallows. Tropical sunlight makes hard shadows; passing showers briefly darken the sea before the colour returns. Boats lift and settle with the swell, their ropes tapping masts above the sound of small waves. People often wear light shirts, dresses and sandals. “Good morning” is a common greeting; “sir” and “ma’am” are polite forms of address.

Bahrain’s flag is red with a white vertical band at the hoist; a zigzag boundary forms five white points facing into the red. Manama combines glass towers, including the twin sail-shaped Bahrain World Trade Center, with low shops, mosques and older limestone buildings. Flat, sandy ground meets the Gulf along reclaimed waterfronts and causeways. Summer light is glaring and the air can be humid; winter is milder. Traffic murmurs beside waterfront promenades, while wind moves palm fronds with a dry rustle. Many men wear white thobes and some women wear abayas, alongside varied contemporary clothing. People greet one another with “السلام عليكم” or “هلا”; “شلونك؟” asks how you are.

Bangladesh’s flag is a dark green field with a red circle slightly toward the hoist from the centre. Dhaka’s crowded streets hold painted cycle rickshaws, concrete buildings, market signs and tangles of overhead wires; outside the cities, broad rivers cut through green rice fields and low, flat land. Monsoon rain drums on tin roofs and raises puddles that reflect headlights. Rickshaw bells ring over traffic noise. People commonly wear saris, salwar kameez, panjabis, lungis or contemporary shirts and trousers, depending on place and occasion. “আসসালামু আলাইকুম” is a common greeting; “কেমন আছেন?” politely asks how someone is. “ভাই” and “আপা” are familiar respectful forms of address.

Barbados’s flag has three equal vertical bands of ultramarine blue, gold and ultramarine blue, with a black broken trident head centred on the gold. In Bridgetown, the stone Parliament Buildings and clock tower stand near narrow streets and harbourfront shops. Elsewhere, small pastel wooden chattel houses sit among palms and flowering shrubs. The west coast has calmer blue water; Atlantic-facing shores receive stronger surf. Bright tropical light falls through moving clouds, and trade winds stir leaves and snap flags while waves break against rock. People wear light everyday clothing, with smart dress for formal occasions. “Good morning” is a common greeting; “sir” and “ma’am” are polite forms of address.

Belarus’s flag has a red upper band occupying two-thirds of its height and a green lower third. Along the hoist runs a vertical white strip bearing a red geometric folk ornament. Minsk has broad avenues, large pale stone and concrete buildings, apartment blocks and the faceted glass National Library. Beyond the cities, mostly flat land holds fields, lakes and birch and pine forests. Winters bring snow, grey skies and the soft crunch of boots; summers are green and often warm. People wear coats, hats and boots in winter, lighter everyday clothes in summer. Greetings include “Добры дзень” in Belarusian and “Здравствуйте” in Russian; “Вы” is a polite form of address.

Belgium’s flag has three equal vertical bands: black at the hoist, yellow, then red. Brussels mixes pale stone civic buildings, glass offices and narrow streets with tram tracks; Bruges has stepped brick gables and canals, while the Ardennes has wooded hills. Overcast skies give façades soft light, and rain darkens cobblestones with a faint hiss under passing bicycles and trams. People wear everyday European coats, jeans and scarves in cool weather. Greetings vary by language: “Goeiedag” and “meneer” in Dutch-speaking areas, “Bonjour” and “madame” in French-speaking areas, and “Guten Tag” and “Herr” in German-speaking areas.

Belize’s flag is blue with narrow red stripes along the top and bottom. At its centre, a white disc holds the coat of arms: two figures beside a shield showing tools and a sailing ship, a mahogany tree above, a green wreath around it and the motto “Sub Umbra Floreo” below. Belize City has low, colourful wooden and concrete buildings, verandas and busy streets; offshore, shallow turquoise water laps against mangroves and reef islands. Heat, bright sun and sudden rain shape the light and sound. People wear light shirts and casual clothes. “Good morning” is common; in Kriol, “Weh di go aan?” is an informal greeting, while “Mister” or “Miss” addresses someone politely.

Benin’s flag has a vertical green band at the hoist; the remaining area is yellow above red in equal horizontal bands. Cotonou’s streets carry motorcycles past concrete shopfronts, market stalls and low buildings beneath a humid coastal sky. Farther north, dry-season light falls on red earth, savanna trees and earth-toned buildings. Motorbike engines buzz, market voices overlap, and rain drums sharply on metal roofs. Clothing ranges from printed cotton garments and headwraps to shirts, trousers and office wear. French is widely used for greetings: “Bonjour, monsieur” or “Bonjour, madame”; people also greet in local languages according to the community.

Bhutan’s flag is divided diagonally from the lower hoist to the upper fly: yellow above and orange below, with a white dragon along the divide holding jewels in its claws. Steep forested mountains frame valleys of whitewashed buildings with carved, painted timber windows and broad roofs; fortress-like dzongs stand above rivers and bridges. Clouds move across ridgelines, changing the light quickly, while river water rushes audibly over rocks. Many people wear modern clothes; traditional dress includes the knee-length gho for men and ankle-length kira for women. A respectful greeting in Dzongkha is “Kuzuzangpo la”; “la” adds politeness when addressing someone.

Bolivia’s flag has three equal horizontal stripes: red, yellow and green from top to bottom. The state version places the national coat of arms at the centre; the plain tricolour is also used. La Paz climbs steep slopes beneath bare Andean peaks, its brick buildings and cable cars crossing thin, bright high-altitude air. Elsewhere, the Salar de Uyuni forms a flat white horizon, while lowland areas are greener and warmer. Cable cars glide almost silently above traffic; wind whistles across open high ground. Dress varies from jackets and jeans to traditional pollera skirts and bowler hats. In Spanish, people say “Buenos días” and address others as “señor” or “señora.”

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s flag is blue with a yellow right triangle and a diagonal line of white five-pointed stars beside it; stars at the ends are cut by the flag’s edges. Sarajevo’s valley holds red-roofed houses, apartment blocks, Ottoman-era lanes and Austro-Hungarian façades beneath wooded hills. In Mostar, pale stone streets lead toward the arched bridge over the green Neretva. Summers can be bright and warm; winter brings low cloud and snow. Footsteps ring on stone, trams rattle in Sarajevo, and river water sounds beneath bridges. People usually wear contemporary casual clothes. “Dobar dan” is a polite greeting; “gospodine” and “gospođo” are respectful forms of address.

Botswana’s flag is light blue with one horizontal black band across the centre, edged above and below by thin white stripes. Gaborone has broad roads, low-rise offices and houses set among dry trees; beyond it, flat grassland and thorn scrub stretch under a wide sky. In the Okavango Delta, reeds and channels reflect pale morning light, with soft splashes from boats and bird calls carrying over the water. Dry-season dust hangs briefly behind moving vehicles; summer storms darken the horizon. People wear everyday shirts, dresses and trousers, with formal wear for offices and occasions. In Setswana, “Dumela” greets one person and “Dumelang” greets several; “Rra” and “Mma” are respectful forms of address.

Brunei’s flag is yellow, crossed diagonally from upper hoist toward lower fly by a broad white band with a narrower black band beneath it. A red national crest sits at the centre, showing a parasol, wings, hands, a crescent and Arabic lettering. Bandar Seri Begawan has low buildings, broad roads and gold-domed mosques reflected in water; stilt houses line parts of the Brunei River. Tropical heat brings intense sun, heavy showers and the patter of rain on roofs. Motorboats hum and leave widening wakes. People wear both modern clothes and Malay dress, including baju kurung and baju Melayu. “Assalamualaikum” is a common greeting; “Tuan” and “Puan” are polite forms of address.

Bulgaria’s flag has three equal horizontal bands: white on top, green in the middle, red below, with no emblem. Sofia has broad boulevards, yellow paving stones near government buildings, domed Orthodox churches, concrete apartment blocks, and Mount Vitosha rising behind the skyline. Elsewhere, villages have plastered houses and red tile roofs; forested mountains and open farmland change from green summers to snowy winters. People wear contemporary European clothes, with heavier coats in cold months. Pedestrians move around trams and cars; their wheels rattle over paving. Daylight can be crisp in winter and warm in summer. Greet someone with Здравейте and address them politely as господин or госпожа.

Burkina Faso’s flag has equal horizontal red and green bands with one yellow five-pointed star at the center. Ouagadougou has low concrete buildings, roadside stalls, motorcycles, and broad dusty streets; beyond the city are dry-season golden grasses, scattered trees, and cultivated fields. In the rainy season, foliage thickens and puddles reflect a pale, cloud-filled sky. People wear shirts and trousers, brightly patterned cotton garments, or long flowing robes, depending on occasion and region. Motorcycles hum and kick up fine reddish dust; market voices carry beneath metal roofs. French is widely used for greetings: Bonjour, monsieur or Bonjour, madame; many people also speak local languages.

Burundi’s flag has a white diagonal cross separating red top and bottom triangles from green left and right triangles. A white disc at its center holds three red six-pointed stars outlined in green. Around Bujumbura, low buildings and busy streets lead toward Lake Tanganyika; inland, steep green hills carry tightly spaced farms and winding roads. Red-brown earth shows at road edges, and rain darkens roofs and foliage. People wear everyday shirts, dresses, and trousers, alongside patterned fabrics for special occasions. Minibuses and motorcycles sound on uneven streets; lakeside water moves in small waves. In Kirundi, greet someone with Bwakeye in the morning or ask Amakuru?; respectful conversation is common.

Cambodia’s flag has blue horizontal bands above and below a red band twice their height; a white depiction of Angkor Wat stands at the center. Phnom Penh mixes riverside promenades, markets, concrete shopfronts, ornate temple roofs, and dense motorcycle traffic. At Angkor, weathered stone towers rise above broad paths and trees; elsewhere, rice fields flatten the landscape beneath a humid sky. People commonly wear light shirts, trousers, skirts, and sandals, with traditional silk clothing for ceremonies. Motorbikes buzz past and rain drums heavily on roofs during the wet season. Greet someone with សួស្តី or the more formal ជំរាបសួរ; លោក and លោកស្រី are respectful forms of address.

Cameroon’s flag has equal vertical green, red, and yellow bands from left to right, with one yellow five-pointed star centered on the red band. Douala has busy roads, markets, port facilities, and humid coastal light; Yaoundé climbs across green hills with concrete buildings and tree-lined streets. Landscapes range from tropical forest and dark volcanic slopes to drier northern grassland. People wear contemporary shirts, dresses, and trousers, as well as colorful patterned fabrics and regionally distinct garments. Taxis and motorcycles weave through traffic, sounding horns; heavy rain splashes against roofs in wetter areas. French and English are official languages: Bonjour, monsieur or madame, and Hello, sir or ma’am, are familiar greetings.

Canada’s flag has a white central square between two equal red vertical bars; a red eleven-pointed maple leaf fills the white field. Toronto has glass towers and streetcars; Montreal has stone facades and metal exterior staircases; many smaller towns have timber houses and broad roads. Landscapes include lakes, forests, prairie, rocky coasts, and snowy mountains, with weather varying greatly by region and season. People dress in everyday contemporary clothes, adding insulated coats and boots in cold weather. Snow muffles footsteps; streetcars ring, and lake water laps at docks. English Hello and French Bonjour are common greetings; people may address others as Mr., Ms., monsieur, or madame.

Cape Verde’s flag is blue with a lower horizontal sequence of white, red, and white stripes; ten yellow five-pointed stars form a circle left of center. Praia has low, pale buildings, paved streets, and views over the Atlantic. Across the islands, dark volcanic rock meets sandy shores, dry hills, and occasional green valleys; wind bends sparse vegetation and drives short waves against the coast. People wear light everyday clothes, with brighter outfits at celebrations. Fishing boats bob at quays, ropes tap against masts, and sea wind rustles awnings. In Portuguese, greet someone with Bom dia and address them as senhor or senhora; Cape Verdean Creole is also widely spoken.

The Central African Republic’s flag has equal blue, white, green, and yellow horizontal bands from top to bottom, a red vertical stripe through their center, and one yellow five-pointed star near the upper-left corner of the blue band. Bangui has low concrete buildings, markets, red-earth roads, and the broad Ubangi River. Beyond it, grassy savanna gives way to wooded areas and southern rainforest. People wear shirts, dresses, trousers, and brightly patterned fabrics; umbrellas appear during heavy rains. Vehicles raise dust in dry weather, while rain patters on corrugated roofs and riverboats hum along the water. In French, Bonjour, monsieur or Bonjour, madame is a polite greeting; Sango is also widely spoken.

Chad’s flag has three equal vertical bands: dark blue at the hoist, yellow, then red, with no emblem. In N’Djamena, low concrete buildings and market awnings spread beside the Chari River; the Grand Mosque’s pale minarets rise above dusty streets. The north is arid, while southern landscapes grow greener during the rains. Harsh midday sun casts short shadows; passing motorcycles buzz, sandals scuff and market voices carry through open air. Clothing varies from flowing robes and wrapped scarves to shirts and trousers. People may greet one another with “السلام عليكم” or “Bonjour,” and address someone politely as “Monsieur” or “Madame.”

Chile’s flag has a white upper band and red lower band; a blue square at the upper hoist holds one white five-pointed star. In Santiago, glass towers, including Gran Torre Santiago, stand against the sharply outlined Andes. Apartment blocks, broad avenues and tree-lined neighbourhood streets sit under dry summer light; farther south, rain darkens wooden houses and lake shores. Metro trains rumble, buses brake and mountain wind stirs leaves. People commonly wear contemporary shirts, jackets and jeans, with warmer layers in winter. Greetings include “Hola” and “Buenos días”; polite forms of address include “señor” and “señora.”

Colombia’s flag has three horizontal bands: yellow across the upper half, blue across the next quarter and red across the bottom quarter, without an emblem. Bogotá sits high among green mountains, with brick buildings, busy avenues and Monserrate rising above its centre. Cartagena looks different: sunlit colonial balconies and thick stone walls near the Caribbean Sea. Afternoon rain can shine on Bogotá’s pavement; buses hiss at stops and street vendors call over traffic. Dress ranges from light coastal clothes to jackets in the cooler capital. People say “Hola,” “Buenos días” or “¿Qué más?” and use “señor” or “señora” politely.

The Comoros flag has four equal horizontal stripes, yellow, white, red and blue from top to bottom. A green triangle at the hoist contains a white crescent and four small white stars arranged vertically between its tips. In Moroni, whitewashed walls and narrow lanes lead toward the harbour, with the Old Friday Mosque beside blue water and Mount Karthala’s volcanic slopes inland. Humid light softens the horizon; waves slap boats, sandals tap stone and market voices mingle with engine noise. People wear varied everyday clothes, including patterned wraps, robes and shirts. Greetings include “السلام عليكم” and “Bonjour”; “Monsieur” and “Madame” are polite forms of address.

The Republic of the Congo’s flag places green at the upper hoist and red at the lower fly, divided by a broad yellow diagonal band running from the lower hoist toward the upper fly. Brazzaville faces Kinshasa across the wide Congo River. Its streets mix low concrete shops, leafy stretches and civic buildings; the Basilica of Sainte-Anne has a distinctive green tiled roof. Humid air softens distant views, while river boats thrum and traffic passes roadside stalls. People wear everything from patterned fabrics to office shirts and jeans. In French, “Bonjour, monsieur” or “Bonjour, madame” is polite; in Lingala, a greeting is “Mbote.”

DR Congo’s flag is sky blue, with a yellow five-pointed star near the upper hoist and a red diagonal band edged in yellow running from lower hoist to upper fly. Kinshasa spreads along the Congo River in broad roads, crowded markets and concrete neighbourhoods; the Palais du Peuple is a prominent civic landmark. Tropical brightness gives way to heavy rain that drums on metal roofs and sends water along kerbs. Buses and motorcycles add engine noise to street conversations. Clothing ranges from tailored, colourful outfits to casual shirts and jeans. Greetings include Lingala “Mbote” and French “Bonjour”; “monsieur” and “madame” are polite addresses.

Costa Rica’s flag has five horizontal bands: blue, white, double-width red, white and blue. The state flag adds the national coat of arms toward the hoist on the red band; plain versions without it are also common. In San José, the ornate National Theatre stands among low-rise shops, buses and traffic. Beyond the city, steep green volcanoes, cloud forest and both Pacific and Caribbean coasts shape the landscape. Rain patters on leaves and roofs; birds call as sunlight breaks through moving clouds. People usually dress in casual shirts, trousers or light jackets. “Hola,” “Buenos días” and “Pura vida” are familiar greetings; “don” and “doña” can precede names respectfully.

Ivory Coast’s flag has three equal vertical bands: orange at the hoist, white in the centre and green at the fly, with no emblem. In Abidjan, glass and concrete towers rise above the Plateau district and the Ébrié Lagoon; Saint Paul’s Cathedral has a striking angled, cable-supported form. Humid sunlight gleams on water and vehicle roofs. Ferries churn across the lagoon, traffic hums on bridges and market conversations spill onto pavements. People wear varied clothing, from patterned dresses and tailored outfits to T-shirts and jeans. French greetings include “Bonjour” and “Bonsoir”; “monsieur” and “madame” are polite forms of address.

Croatia’s flag has three horizontal stripes, red, white and blue, with a central red-and-white checkerboard shield topped by five small heraldic shields. Along the Adriatic, pale limestone streets and terracotta roofs meet clear blue water; Dubrovnik’s stone walls rise above a compact old town. Inland, Zagreb has tram tracks, broad squares and Austro-Hungarian façades. Summers are bright and dry on the coast; winters can be grey and cold inland. People generally wear contemporary casual clothes, with light layers by the sea. Footsteps tap on polished stone, trams rattle, and boat ropes creak. People greet with “Dobar dan” or informal “Bok”; respectful address includes “gospodine” and “gospođo.”

The Republic of Cyprus flag is white, with a copper-orange silhouette of the island above two crossed green olive branches. Cyprus has dry golden hills, olive and carob trees, rocky shores and bright turquoise shallows. Nicosia’s streets mix pale stone buildings, modern shopfronts and shaded cafés; coastal towns have apartment blocks, harbours and low-rise houses. Summer sun is intense, while winters are milder and sometimes rainy. People commonly wear modern, lightweight clothes, adding jackets in cooler months. Cicadas buzz in dry vegetation and café cups clink on terraces. Greek speakers greet with “Γεια σας” and may say “κύριε” or “κυρία”; Turkish speakers use “Merhaba” and “bey” or “hanım.”

The Czech Republic’s flag has a white upper half, red lower half and blue triangle extending from the hoist to the centre. Prague’s skyline has copper-green domes, church spires, red roofs and the stone arches of Charles Bridge over the Vltava. Smaller towns often have coloured plaster façades around paved squares; elsewhere, forests and rolling fields frame roads and villages. Winter brings low light and sometimes snow; summer brings long, warm evenings. People wear contemporary coats, scarves or casual summer clothes according to season. Trams squeal around bends and footsteps click on paving stones. “Dobrý den” is a polite greeting, “Ahoj” informal; “pane” and “paní” are respectful forms of address.

Denmark’s flag is red with a white Nordic cross whose vertical bar sits closer to the hoist. Copenhagen has narrow colourful waterfront houses, brick apartment blocks, cycle lanes and low, mostly flat skylines. Outside cities are fields, beech woods, sandy coasts and small harbours. Light is soft under frequent cloud; wind moves flags, grasses and bicycle jackets, and winter afternoons darken early. People typically wear practical contemporary clothing, often layered for rain and wind. Bicycle tyres hiss on damp pavement, bells ring, and harbour rigging taps against masts. People say “Hej” or “Goddag”; first names and the informal pronoun “du” are common in everyday address.

Djibouti’s flag has a light blue upper stripe and green lower stripe, with a white triangle at the hoist bearing a red five-pointed star. Djibouti City has pale concrete buildings, busy paved streets, port cranes and waterfront views across the Gulf of Tadjoura. Inland, volcanic rock, dry plains and salt-white shores sit under hard sunlight and heat haze. People wear varied clothing, including light shirts and trousers, Somali garments, headscarves and flowing robes. Engines idle near the port; wind brushes over gravel and the call to prayer carries across neighbourhoods. Greetings include Arabic “السلام عليكم,” Somali “Nabad,” and French “Bonjour”; polite address may use “سيد” or “سيدة,” or “monsieur” and “madame.”

The Dominican Republic’s flag has a white cross dividing four rectangles: blue at upper hoist and lower fly, red at upper fly and lower hoist. Its central coat of arms includes a Bible, cross, laurel and palm branches. Santo Domingo combines limestone colonial buildings and plazas with traffic-filled avenues and modern towers. Elsewhere, palms edge sandy coasts, while green mountains rise inland. Tropical sun makes crisp shadows; afternoon showers bring steam off warm streets. People wear contemporary lightweight clothes, with smarter shirts or dresses for work and celebrations. Motorcycles buzz, waves break and music drifts from shops. People greet with “Hola” or “Buenos días”; “señor” and “señora” are polite forms of address.

Ecuador’s flag has horizontal yellow, blue and red bands; yellow occupies the top half, with the national coat of arms centered over the bands. The coat shows a condor above a shield with a mountain, river and steamship. Quito’s steep streets climb between pale colonial buildings and concrete apartment blocks, with Andean mountains beyond; coastal Guayaquil is flatter, warmer and lined with palms. Thin mountain sunlight casts sharp shadows, while afternoon clouds soften the view. Buses brake with a hiss and market sellers call across tiled sidewalks. Dress ranges from jeans and jackets to regionally specific woven garments. People greet each other with “Hola” or “Buenos días,” addressing strangers as “señor” or “señora.”

El Salvador’s flag has three equal horizontal bands, blue, white and blue, with the national coat of arms centered on the white band: a triangle containing five volcanoes, topped by a red liberty cap and rainbow, within a circular inscription. San Salvador mixes low concrete shopfronts, traffic-filled avenues and leafy neighborhoods beneath volcanic slopes. Beyond the capital are compact towns, cultivated hills and Pacific beaches with dark volcanic sand. Tropical sun makes hard midday shadows; rain runs quickly along gutters in wet season. Buses rumble, birds call and market conversations overlap. People commonly wear lightweight shirts, jeans and work uniforms. “Buenos días” is a polite greeting; “don” or “doña” may precede an older person’s name.

Equatorial Guinea’s flag has horizontal green, white and red stripes and a blue triangle extending from the hoist. Centered on the white stripe is a coat of arms showing a silk-cotton tree beneath six yellow stars. Malabo has humid, leafy streets, painted concrete buildings and older façades near the waterfront; mainland Bata has broad roads, markets and an Atlantic shore. Dense green vegetation grows close to settlements, and rain leaves a sheen on roofs and pavement. Traffic hum, insects buzz and sudden showers drum on metal awnings. People wear everyday shirts, dresses and business clothes, with brighter patterned fabrics also common. In Spanish, people greet each other with “Hola” or “Buenos días” and address strangers as “señor” or “señora.”

Eritrea’s flag forms a red triangle widening from the hoist to the fly, with green above and blue below; a gold olive wreath encircling an upright branch sits in the red near the hoist. Asmara’s streets have cream and pastel façades, balconies, cafés and broad avenues, set on a high plateau with clear, dry light. Toward the Red Sea, the land becomes hotter and drier, with pale coastal buildings and sparse vegetation. Loose fabric lifts in the breeze; footsteps, conversation and café cups sound along the pavement. Clothing includes shirts, trousers, dresses and traditional garments for gatherings. In Tigrinya, “Selam” is a greeting; “Kemey aleka?” asks a familiar man how he is.

Estonia’s flag is three equal horizontal bands: blue on top, black in the middle and white below, with no emblem. Tallinn’s old town has steep red-tiled roofs, limestone walls and narrow cobbled lanes; outside it stand apartment blocks, glass offices and tram-lined streets. Flat countryside opens into forests, bogs and a low Baltic coastline. Winter light is brief and blue-gray, with snow muffling steps; summer evenings remain bright and long. Trams ring softly at crossings, shoes click on stone and wind rustles birch leaves. People dress in coats and boots in cold months, lighter everyday clothes in summer. “Tere” means hello; “Tere päevast” is more formal, and “härra” or “proua” are polite forms of address.

Eswatini’s flag has a broad red central band between narrow yellow bands and outer blue bands. Its center bears a black-and-white shield, two spears and a staff with feather ornaments. Around Mbabane, roads curve through green hills past low shops, homes and government buildings; in warmer lowlands, fields and scattered trees stretch beneath wide skies. Sunlight is bright, and summer rain darkens red earth and makes roadside grass shine. Minibuses idle, tires hiss on wet roads and birds call from trees. Everyday clothing includes shirts, skirts, trousers and school uniforms; traditional attire appears at ceremonies. In siSwati, “Sawubona” greets one person and “Sanibonani” greets several; “Babe” and “Make” can respectfully address elders.

Ethiopia’s flag has equal horizontal green, yellow and red bands, with a blue circle and gold five-point star at the center; gold rays extend between the star’s points. Addis Ababa combines high-rise construction, concrete apartments, busy roads and tree-lined compounds on a high plateau. Beyond it, landscapes range from rugged green highlands to dry lowlands. The highland sun is strong, but mornings can feel cool; rainy-season clouds soften distant hills. Minibuses call for passengers, traffic murmurs and coffee cups clink in cafés. People wear contemporary shirts, dresses and jackets, with white woven garments common at celebrations. In Amharic, “Selam” means hello; “Indet newot?” politely asks how someone is, and “Ato” or “Woyzero” may precede a name.

Fiji’s light-blue flag carries the Union Jack in the upper hoist corner and a shield on the fly side. The shield has a red cross, a gold lion above it, and panels showing sugar cane, a coconut palm, bananas and a white dove. Suva has waterfront roads, covered markets, low commercial buildings and green hills close behind; elsewhere, villages, farms and beaches sit among lush tropical vegetation. Humid daylight glints on water, and passing showers make roofs and leaves shine. Waves wash against shorelines while buses rumble and market vendors talk. Everyday dress includes light shirts, dresses and sulu wrap skirts. “Bula” is a common greeting; “turaga” and “marama” are respectful forms of address.

Finland’s flag is white with a blue Nordic cross extending to the edges, its vertical bar offset toward the hoist. Helsinki has pale stone civic buildings, tram wires, harbours and compact blocks of cream and ochre apartments. Elsewhere, dark spruce and pine surround still lakes, wooden cottages and low granite shores. Winter light is brief and blue-grey; snow muffles footsteps and tyres crunch on packed ice. Summer evenings stay bright, with gulls calling over the water. People wear practical coats and boots in winter, lighter layers in summer. Greetings include Finnish “hei” and “hyvää päivää,” and Swedish “hej”; formal address may use “herra” or “rouva.”

Gabon’s flag has three equal horizontal bands: green above yellow above blue, with no emblem. Libreville faces the Atlantic with broad roads, low commercial buildings, glass-fronted offices and palms near the waterfront. Beyond the capital, dense green rainforest meets red earth roads, rivers and humid beaches. Rain darkens the pavement and drums loudly on metal roofs; in dry spells, warm haze softens the light. People commonly wear shirts, dresses and trousers, with colourful printed fabrics also visible at gatherings and markets. In French, a common greeting is “bonjour”; people may address someone politely as “monsieur” or “madame.”

Gambia’s flag has horizontal red, blue and green bands, with a narrow white stripe separating blue from each outer colour. The River Gambia winds through flat land edged by mangroves, fields and villages; near Banjul are sandy streets, markets, low buildings and Atlantic beaches. Dry-season light can be dusty and golden, while rain brings bright greenery and puddles. Wooden boats rock at their moorings, outboard motors buzz, and market voices carry through open stalls. People wear everyday shirts and trousers as well as flowing, brightly coloured garments. Greetings vary by language: “salaam aleekum” is widely understood, and Wolof speakers may say “nanga def?”

Georgia’s flag is white with one large red cross reaching all four edges and four smaller red crosses, one in each white quarter. Tbilisi climbs steep hills beside the Mtkvari River, with carved wooden balconies, stone churches, apartment blocks and a modern glass bridge. Beyond the city, the Caucasus rises into sharp, snowy peaks above valleys and vineyards. Cars hum over uneven streets; church bells may ring across rooftops. Light shifts quickly between bright sun and mountain cloud. People wear contemporary jackets, dresses and jeans. A Georgian greeting is “გამარჯობა” (gamarjoba); polite forms of address include “ბატონო” (batono) and “ქალბატონო” (kalbatono).

Ghana’s flag has equal horizontal red, yellow and green bands, with a single black five-pointed star centred in the yellow band. Accra mixes concrete shopfronts, roadside stalls, modern towers and busy roads near the coast. Farther inland are green farms, forest and, in the north, more open savanna. Sunlight is strong, softened at times by humid cloud or dry-season haze. Traffic horns, market calls and rain striking corrugated roofs are familiar sounds. People wear shirts, jeans and dresses, alongside vividly patterned cloth and tailored garments. English greetings include “good morning”; in Twi, “maakye” means good morning, and “nana” is a respectful address for a chief or elder.

Greece’s flag has nine alternating blue and white horizontal stripes, beginning and ending blue, with a white cross on a blue square in the upper hoist corner. Athens has pale apartment blocks, balconies, narrow streets and the Acropolis rising above the roofs. Islands often show whitewashed walls, blue shutters, dry hills and clear water against rocky shores. Summer light is hard and bright; cicadas rasp in the heat, while ferries rumble and ropes creak at harbours. People generally wear contemporary casual clothes, with lighter fabrics in summer. “Γεια σας” (yia sas) is a polite greeting; “κύριε” (kyrie) and “κυρία” (kyria) address a man or woman respectfully.

Grenada’s flag has a red border bearing six yellow five-pointed stars, three along the top and three along the bottom. Inside, yellow triangles fill the top and bottom, green triangles the sides, and a red central disk holds one yellow star; a nutmeg symbol sits on the left green triangle. St. George’s curves around a harbour, with pastel buildings and red roofs climbing green hills. Elsewhere are steep roads, rainforest, beaches and small fishing boats. Tropical sun makes colours vivid; showers patter on roofs and waves slap against docks. People wear casual light clothing. English greetings include “good morning” and “how you doing?”; “Mr.” and “Miss” are familiar respectful forms.

Guatemala’s flag has three equal vertical bands, light blue, white and light blue. Centred on the white band, its coat of arms shows a green quetzal on a dated parchment scroll, with crossed rifles, crossed swords and a laurel wreath. Guatemala City has concrete buildings and busy roads, while Antigua has cobbled streets, coloured plaster façades and volcanoes on the horizon. Highland towns sit among pine-covered slopes; lowland areas are warmer and greener. Afternoon rain can drum on tile roofs, followed by clear, sharp light. People wear contemporary clothing, and some wear distinctive locally woven textiles. Spanish greetings include “hola” and “buenos días”; respectful address uses “señor,” “señora” and “usted.”

Guinea’s flag has three equal vertical bands: red at the hoist, yellow in the middle, green at the fly. In Conakry, low concrete buildings and market stalls crowd streets near the Atlantic; farther inland, green hills rise around the Fouta Djallon highlands. Rains darken the roads and bead on corrugated roofs, while the dry season brings dust and sharp sunlight. People wear everyday shirts, trousers and dresses, alongside patterned boubous and headwraps. Taxis brake and weave around pedestrians, with horns and market calls filling the air. In French, people greet one another with “Bonjour” and may address a stranger as “monsieur” or “madame.”

Guinea-Bissau’s flag has a red vertical band at the hoist bearing a black five-pointed star; the remaining area is yellow above green in two equal horizontal bands. Bissau has low, pastel-painted buildings, sandy roadside shoulders, broad trees and a waterfront of small boats. Beyond the capital lie mangroves, rice fields and the low islands of the Bijagós archipelago. Humid light softens colours; rain makes unpaved roads muddy. People wear light shirts, dresses, patterned cloth and headwraps. Engines buzz, boats knock against docks and conversations carry across markets. In Portuguese, a greeting is “Bom dia”; polite forms of address include “senhor” and “senhora.”

Guyana’s flag is green with a long yellow arrowhead outlined in black pointing from the hoist toward the fly; a shorter red triangle, edged in white, sits inside it at the hoist. Georgetown’s wooden houses often stand on stilts, with louvered windows, verandas, canals and broad avenues. Away from the coast are dense rainforest, wide rivers and savanna. Tropical rain drums on metal roofs, then bright sun reflects from wet pavement. People dress in shirts, trousers, dresses and workwear suited to the heat. Minibuses hum past market stalls. English greetings include “Good morning” and the conversational “How yuh doin’?”; “sir” and “miss” are familiar forms of address.

Haiti’s flag has equal blue and red horizontal bands, blue above red. Its state flag carries a central white panel with the coat of arms: a palm topped by a liberty cap, surrounded by flags, cannons and other emblems, above a ribbon reading “L’Union Fait La Force.” In Port-au-Prince, painted concrete buildings climb steep hills above busy streets; elsewhere, mountains frame coastal towns and bright sea. Strong sun casts hard shadows, while sudden rain runs down slopes. People wear practical everyday clothes, colourful dresses and headwraps. Street vendors call over engines and music. In Haitian Creole, people say “Bonjou, kòman ou ye?” and address others as “mesye” or “madanm.”

Honduras’s flag has three equal horizontal bands, blue, white and blue, with five blue five-pointed stars arranged like an X in the centre of the white band. Tegucigalpa spreads across steep hills, its concrete neighbourhoods threaded by winding roads; low colonial-era buildings and churches punctuate older streets. Beyond the cities are pine-covered mountains, tropical forest and Caribbean beaches. Afternoon sun can be intense, and rainwater rushes along sloped streets. People wear shirts, jeans, dresses and school or work uniforms. Buses rumble, vendors call and birds sound from roadside trees. In Spanish, “Buenos días, ¿cómo está?” is a polite greeting; “señor” and “señora” are respectful forms of address.

Hungary’s flag has three equal horizontal stripes: red on top, white in the middle and green below, with no emblem on the national flag. In Budapest, the Danube separates hilly Buda from flatter Pest; stone bridges, the domed Parliament building, tram wires and ornate apartment façades shape the view. Elsewhere, broad plains and small towns stretch beneath open skies. Summer light is warm, while winter can bring grey skies and snow. People wear familiar European street clothes, adding coats, scarves and boots in cold weather. Trams clatter on rails and café cups click indoors. In Hungarian, a polite greeting is “Jó napot kívánok”; “uram” addresses a man respectfully.

Iceland’s blue flag carries a white-edged red Nordic cross, its vertical arm set closer to the hoist than the fly. Reykjavík has low, colourful houses, corrugated-metal roofs and the pale concrete spire of Hallgrímskirkja above compact streets. Outside towns, dark lava fields, moss, waterfalls and distant glaciers sit under rapidly changing skies. Wind pushes rain sideways and ripples harbour water; winter light stays low, while summer evenings remain bright. People wear layered jackets, knitwear and sturdy shoes. Waves slap quays, and wind whistles around building corners. In Icelandic, people say “Góðan daginn” or “Hæ” and commonly address one another by first name.

Indonesia’s flag is a plain rectangle of two equal horizontal bands, red above white, without an emblem. Jakarta’s skyline mixes glass towers, elevated roads, mosques, shops and dense residential streets; across the islands, landscapes range from rice terraces and volcanic slopes to mangroves and beaches. Humid daylight makes leaves glossy, and tropical downpours drum on roofs and pool beside curbs. Motorbikes flow around slower traffic, their engines blending with street vendors’ calls. People wear varied everyday clothes; batik shirts and dresses are common, and many women wear hijabs. In Indonesian, “Selamat pagi” means good morning; “Pak” and “Bu” are respectful ways to address adults.

Ireland’s flag has three equal vertical bands: green at the hoist, white, then orange, with no emblem. Dublin mixes Georgian brick terraces, painted doors and stone public buildings with glass offices; beyond it are hedged fields, low stone walls, Atlantic cliffs and small towns with plaster storefronts. Moist air softens the light, and showers can darken pavement within minutes. People usually wear ordinary modern clothes with rain jackets close at hand. Footsteps sound sharp on wet stone; buses hiss at stops, while wind and seabirds carry along the coast. Greetings include “Howya?” in English and “Dia duit” in Irish; “a chara” means “dear friend” in Irish address.

Jamaica’s flag is divided by a gold diagonal cross: green triangles above and below, black triangles at the hoist and fly. Kingston has low concrete shops, bright signs, roadside stalls and hills rising behind denser blocks; elsewhere, narrow roads curve through green mountains toward pale beaches and turquoise water. Sunlight is strong, with hard midday shadows and brief heavy showers. People wear varied everyday clothes, from office shirts to T-shirts and sandals. Minibuses rumble, vendors call out, and tree frogs sound after rain. “Wah gwaan?” is an informal greeting; “Mawnin” means good morning. People may address someone respectfully as “Miss” or “Mister.”

Kazakhstan’s sky-blue flag bears a gold sun with 32 rays above a soaring gold eagle; a vertical gold ornamental pattern runs beside the hoist. Astana has broad avenues and striking glass-and-metal towers, while Almaty has tree-lined streets beneath snowy mountains. Open steppe stretches under an enormous sky, and winters bring compacted snow and visible breath; summers can be hot and dry. People wear contemporary coats, business clothes or casual wear, with warmer layers in winter. Trams and traffic hum in cities; wind moves audibly through steppe grass. A polite Kazakh greeting is “Сәлеметсіз бе?” An older man may be addressed as “аға,” an older woman as “апай.”

Kenya’s flag has horizontal black, red and green bands separated by narrow white stripes. At its centre is a red, black and white Maasai shield with two crossed white spears. Nairobi’s skyline rises above busy roads, markets and leafy neighbourhoods; elsewhere are tea-covered hills, dry savanna, highlands and a humid Indian Ocean coast. Equatorial daylight is bright, though altitude and season change the temperature markedly. People wear varied modern clothing, with regional dress also seen at ceremonies and in daily life. Matatus brake and play music; insects and birds fill quieter landscapes. In Swahili, people greet each other with “Habari?” and may say “Shikamoo” to an elder, addressing him respectfully as “mzee.”

Kiribati’s flag has a red upper half with a yellow frigatebird above a rising yellow sun with 17 rays. Its blue lower half carries three white wavy horizontal stripes. On South Tarawa, narrow roads and causeways link low coral islets; houses, small shops and coconut palms sit close to both lagoon and ocean. Other atolls have sandy paths and broad, shallow lagoons. Tropical sun makes short shadows at midday, while trade winds bend palm fronds and rattle roofing; waves sound against reef edges. People commonly wear light shirts, skirts or shorts. In Gilbertese, “Mauri” is a greeting; “Unimwane” and “Unaine” respectfully refer to elder men and women.

Kyrgyzstan’s red flag shows a yellow sun with 40 straight rays. At its centre is a red tunduk, the crossed roof opening of a yurt, set within the yellow sun. Bishkek has wide, tree-shaded avenues, apartment blocks and mountain views; outside cities, steep green summer pastures rise to rocky peaks and snowfields. Winters are cold, while highland weather can shift quickly. People usually wear contemporary clothes; felt kalpaks and embroidered garments appear on particular occasions. Traffic hums beneath city trees, and wind brushes grass around grazing animals. “Саламатсызбы” is a polite Kyrgyz greeting; “агай” and “эжей” are respectful forms of address, often used for teachers.

Laos’s flag has horizontal red, blue and red bands in a 1:2:1 height ratio, with a large white circle centred on the blue band. Vientiane has low-rise shopfronts, broad roads, riverside promenades and gilded temple roofs. Beyond it, forested hills frame the Mekong and its tributaries; rice fields turn vivid green in the wet season. Humid light can look hazy, followed by hard tropical rain. People wear everyday modern clothes; some women wear a woven sinh skirt, especially at work or formal gatherings. Motorbikes buzz past market stalls, and temple bells carry softly. “ສະບາຍດີ” is a greeting; “ອ້າຍ” addresses an older man and “ເອື້ອຍ” an older woman.

Latvia’s flag has three horizontal stripes: deep carmine red, white, then carmine red, in a 2:1:2 height ratio, with no emblem. Riga combines a skyline of church spires, Art Nouveau façades, stone-paved old streets and later apartment blocks. Beyond the capital are pine forests, flat farmland and sandy Baltic beaches. Winter light is low and brief, with snow and slush; summer evenings stay bright for hours. People wear contemporary clothes, adding substantial coats, hats and boots in cold weather. Trams squeal on curves, shoes scrape on icy pavement, and wind moves through coastal pines. “Labdien” is a polite Latvian greeting; “kungs” means sir and “kundze” means madam.

Lesotho’s flag has three equal horizontal bands of blue, white and green, with a black Basotho hat centered on the white band. Around Maseru, low brick and stone buildings sit below bare, rolling highlands; farther out, round stone houses and steep mountain roads are common. Winter light is crisp, with snow possible on high peaks. People wear everyday shirts and jackets, while patterned Basotho blankets and conical straw hats appear in colder weather and cultural settings. Footsteps crunch on gravel, sheep bleat, and wind moves through dry grass. In Sesotho, people greet one another with “Lumela,” addressing elders respectfully as “ntate” or “’mè.”

Liberia’s flag has eleven alternating red and white horizontal stripes, red at the top and bottom, and a blue square in the upper hoist corner containing one white five-pointed star. Monrovia has busy paved roads, painted concrete shops, corrugated roofs and a humid Atlantic waterfront; beyond the capital are dense green forests and palm-lined beaches. Heavy rain darkens the pavement, while midday sun reflects sharply off metal roofs. People wear T-shirts, dresses, office clothes and brightly patterned fabrics. Traffic hums, market vendors call, and surf breaks along the shore. Liberian English greetings include “How you doing?”; “Ma” and “Pa” can be respectful forms of address.

Libya’s flag has a red upper band, a black middle band twice its height, and a green lower band; a white crescent and five-pointed star sit at the center of the black band. Tripoli’s white and cream buildings, arcaded streets and old medina meet a bright Mediterranean coast. Inland, towns give way to broad, stony desert and dunes beneath a pale, often cloudless sky. People wear contemporary shirts and dresses, with some men in long robes and women in varied styles of headscarf. Cars pass over dusty roads, market voices carry, and sea wind rustles palms. Common greetings are “السلام عليكم” and “وعليكم السلام”; “يا خوي” is a familiar address.

Liechtenstein’s flag has two equal horizontal bands, blue above red, with a small gold crown near the hoist on the blue band. Vaduz Castle stands on a wooded slope above a compact town of pale plaster buildings, pitched roofs and tidy streets. The Rhine valley is flat and green, bordered by steep Alpine mountains; winter snow brightens the peaks, while summer light is clear. People generally wear contemporary European clothes, adding sturdy coats and boots in cold weather. Bicycle tires hiss on pavement, church bells ring, and mountain streams rush after rain. People may greet each other with “Hoi” or “Guten Tag,” using “Herr” or “Frau” in formal address.

Lithuania’s flag consists of three equal horizontal bands: yellow on top, green in the middle and red below. Vilnius has pale Baroque façades, narrow old-town streets and the red-brick Gediminas Tower above the Neris and Vilnia rivers. Outside the cities, flat fields, pine woods and Baltic dunes stretch under changeable skies. Summer light stays late; winters bring low sun, frost and occasional snow. People wear everyday European street clothes, with heavy coats and scarves in winter. Trolleybuses hum, shoes tap on cobbles, and leaves rustle in courtyard trees. In Lithuanian, “Labas” is informal, “Laba diena” is polite, and “pone” or “ponia” addresses someone respectfully.

Luxembourg’s flag has three equal horizontal bands of red, white and light blue, noticeably paler than the blue on the Dutch flag. Luxembourg City rises over deep green valleys, with stone fortifications, arched bridges, pale façades and modern glass offices. Beyond it are wooded hills, villages with steep roofs and vineyards along the Moselle. Rain can leave the stone streets glossy; winter skies are often gray, while summer evenings are long and mild. People wear contemporary European clothes and practical raincoats. Trams glide quietly, footsteps echo beneath arches, and café conversations mix languages. In Luxembourgish, “Moien” means hello; “Här” and “Madamm” are respectful forms of address.

Madagascar’s flag has a vertical white band at the hoist; the remaining area is divided horizontally, red above green. Antananarivo climbs steep hills with red-earth lanes, brick houses, balconies and crowded markets. Terraced rice paddies spread through the highlands, while baobabs stand in the drier west and tropical forests grow farther east. Highland mornings can be cool and misty; coastal light is warmer and brighter. People wear contemporary clothes, and some wrap patterned lamba cloth around their shoulders. Vendors call over traffic, zebu carts creak, and rain patters on metal roofs. In Malagasy, “Salama” and “Manao ahoana” are greetings; “tompoko” adds respect.

Malawi’s flag has three equal horizontal bands, black above red above green, with a red rising sun and its rays centered in the black band. Lilongwe has leafy avenues, low concrete buildings, market stalls and minibuses; farther east, Lake Malawi meets sandy beaches and clear blue water. Wooded hills, farmland and tea-green slopes shape other regions. The dry season brings bright, dusty light, while rains turn roadside vegetation vivid green. People wear everyday shirts, dresses and patterned chitenje wraps. Minibus conductors call destinations, market chatter overlaps, and small waves lap the lakeshore. In Chichewa, people say “Moni” or “Muli bwanji?”; “Amai” and “Abambo” are respectful addresses.

Malaysia’s flag has 14 alternating red and white horizontal stripes and a blue canton containing a yellow crescent and 14-point star. Kuala Lumpur rises with glass towers, including the twin Petronas Towers, above shopfronts and busy roads; elsewhere, timber houses, palms and dense rainforest frame humid streets. Afternoon light is bright, then rain darkens the pavement and drums on metal roofs. People wear T-shirts, office clothes, baju kurung, batik shirts and headscarves, depending on setting. Traffic hums and food stalls clatter. In Malay, people say “Selamat pagi” or “Apa khabar?” and respectfully address someone as “Encik” or “Puan.”

The Maldives flag is a red field with a centered green rectangle and a white crescent opening toward the fly. Low islands sit barely above turquoise water: pale sand, coconut palms, jetties and boats, with Malé’s closely packed mid-rise buildings forming a different, denser skyline. Sunlight glitters sharply on ripples; waves slide quietly over sand while outboard motors buzz offshore. Clothing ranges from light resort wear to everyday shirts, long dresses and headscarves in inhabited communities. Boats pitch and tug against mooring ropes. In Dhivehi, “Assalaamu alaikum” is a greeting and “Kihineh?” asks how someone is; visitors may be addressed as “sir” or “madam.”

Mali’s flag has three equal vertical bands: green at the hoist, yellow in the middle and red at the fly. Bamako has low concrete buildings, market roofs and roads busy with motorbikes beside the Niger River. Farther north, ochre earth, Sahel scrub and sun-baked mud-brick buildings replace the greener riverbanks. Dry-season light is dusty and hard-edged; rain makes unpaved ground dark and slippery. People wear tailored shirts and trousers, patterned cloth, flowing boubous and head coverings. Engines buzz, vendors call and sandals scrape on gritty ground. In Bambara, “I ni sogoma” means good morning; in French, people say “Bonjour, monsieur” or “Bonjour, madame.”

Malta’s flag has equal vertical white and red bands, with a small grey George Cross, outlined in red, in the upper hoist corner. Valletta’s pale limestone walls, church domes and enclosed wooden balconies step toward a blue harbour; narrow streets throw crisp shadows under strong Mediterranean sun. Buses and small cars thread past stone façades, while ferries churn the water and church bells carry across the streets. Summer clothing is light; office wear and jackets appear in cooler months. Greetings in Maltese include “Bonġu” for good morning, while “Sur” and “Sinjura” are respectful ways to address a man or woman.

The Marshall Islands flag has a deep blue field, widening diagonal orange and white bands running from the lower hoist toward the upper fly, and a white 24-point star near the hoist above them. On Majuro, a narrow strip of land holds low buildings, roadside shops and palms between lagoon water and open ocean. Bright tropical light catches corrugated roofs; passing showers soften the horizon. People wear casual shirts, shorts, skirts and dresses, sometimes with woven accessories. Waves break against the ocean shore, boats knock against docks and wind rattles palm fronds. In Marshallese, people greet one another with “Iakwe” and may say “Iakwe eok” to greet someone directly.

Mauritania’s flag is green with narrow red horizontal bands along the top and bottom; a gold crescent opening upward sits below a gold five-point star. Nouakchott spreads in low, pale concrete blocks and sandy streets near the Atlantic, with shop signs and market awnings interrupting the flat skyline. Inland, dunes and stony plains meet a wide, often hazy sky. Wind moves loose sand across roads, and traffic, market voices and the ocean surf provide the sound. People wear shirts and trousers, flowing daraa robes, melhfa wraps and headscarves. Greetings commonly begin “السلام عليكم,” answered “وعليكم السلام”; “سيدي” is a respectful form of address.

Mauritius’s flag has four equal horizontal bands, red, blue, yellow and green from top to bottom. Port Louis combines low colonial-era buildings, modern offices and market streets against steep green mountains; elsewhere, sugarcane fields run toward beaches and shallow lagoons. Tropical sunlight makes painted walls vivid, while brief rain leaves roads reflective. People wear everyday shirts, dresses and office clothes, with saris, salwar kameez and other dress visible according to occasion. Buses rumble, market sellers call and waves hiss across reef-protected sand. In Mauritian Creole, “Bonzour” is a greeting; “Misie” and “Madam” are respectful ways to address someone.

Mexico’s flag has equal vertical green, white and red bands, with the national coat of arms centered on the white: an eagle holding a snake while perched on a cactus above water. Mexico City mixes broad avenues, stone civic buildings, apartment blocks and distant mountains; other regions have deserts, forests, coastal towns and brightly painted houses. High-altitude sunlight casts sharp shadows, while market awnings make pools of colour. People wear varied everyday clothes, from jeans and workwear to embroidered garments for particular communities and occasions. Traffic rolls past street vendors calling out orders. In Spanish, people greet others with “Buenos días” and address them respectfully as “señor” or “señora.”

The Federated States of Micronesia flies a light-blue flag with four white five-pointed stars arranged like a diamond around its centre. On Pohnpei, low concrete buildings with corrugated roofs line wet streets near green hills and mangroves; elsewhere, narrow roads pass palms, lagoons and small harbours. Rain clouds can arrive quickly, turning bright tropical light soft and grey. People commonly wear T-shirts, shorts, light dresses or skirts. Languages vary between islands: on Pohnpei, people may greet someone with “Kaselehlie”; English “hello” is also common, with “Mr.” or “Ms.” in formal address. Outboard motors buzz across water, and palms bend in coastal wind.

Moldova’s flag has equal vertical blue, yellow and red bands from the hoist, with its coat of arms centred on the yellow: an eagle holding a cross in its beak, an olive branch and sceptre in its claws, and a chest shield bearing an aurochs head, star, rose and crescent. Chișinău has broad, tree-lined streets, pale stone civic buildings and apartment blocks; villages have plastered houses, orchards and vineyards. Summers are warm and leafy, winters grey and sometimes snowy. People wear ordinary European street clothes and heavier coats in winter. “Bună ziua” is a polite greeting; “domnule” addresses a man and “doamnă” a woman. Trolleybuses hum and vineyard leaves rustle.

Monaco’s flag is two equal horizontal bands, red above white, with no emblem. Its narrow Mediterranean coastline is packed with pale apartment towers, stepped terraces and roads curving around steep rock. Port Hercules holds tightly moored boats; the Prince’s Palace rises above the old town, while the Casino de Monte-Carlo has ornate stonework and domes. Strong sun reflects off cream façades and blue water. People wear everyday summer shirts, dresses and sunglasses, with formal clothes at some evening venues. In French, “Bonjour” is a common greeting; “Monsieur” and “Madame” are polite forms of address. Traffic rolls through tunnels, and boat lines creak against quays.

Mongolia’s flag has equal vertical red, blue and red bands, with a yellow Soyombo symbol on the hoist-side red band. Ulaanbaatar mixes glass offices, concrete apartment blocks and hillside ger districts. Beyond it, open grassland rolls toward bare mountains; round white gers have low doors, felt coverings and ropes that tug in the wind. Winter light is sharp over snow, while summer brings green pasture and dust from unpaved tracks. City residents wear contemporary coats and street clothes; a colourful deel appears at celebrations and in rural settings. “Сайн байна уу?” greets someone politely; “ах” and “эгч” respectfully address an older man or woman. Hooves thud softly on turf.

Montenegro’s flag is red with a thin gold border and a gold double-headed eagle at its centre; the eagle bears a shield showing a gold lion on blue and green. Along the Bay of Kotor, limestone mountains rise behind stone houses, red-tiled roofs and narrow waterfront roads. Inland, darker forests and the Durmitor mountains bring cooler air; the Adriatic coast has bright, dry summer light. People usually wear casual European clothes, with jackets in mountain towns or winter. “Dobar dan” is a polite greeting, while “gospodine” and “gospođo” address a man and woman respectfully. Church bells carry across bays, and small boats knock gently against docks.

Mozambique’s flag has horizontal green, black and yellow bands separated by narrow white stripes. A red triangle at the hoist contains a yellow star, an open white book, and crossed hoe and rifle as emblems. Maputo has broad avenues, concrete apartment buildings, older balconied façades and a palm-lined waterfront; farther along the coast are sandy beaches, fishing boats and mangroves. Tropical light is strong, with humid rainy periods. People wear shirts, trousers and dresses; colourful capulana cloth is wrapped as a skirt or used to carry a child. In Portuguese, “Bom dia” greets someone in the morning; “senhor” and “senhora” are polite forms of address. Minibuses rumble past, and surf breaks steadily.

Myanmar’s flag has three equal horizontal bands of yellow, green and red, with a large white five-pointed star centred across them. In Yangon, the gold-clad Shwedagon Pagoda rises above trees and crowded streets of older masonry buildings and newer towers. Bagan’s brick pagodas spread across a dry plain, while rural roads pass fields and stilted wooden homes. Sunlight can be hazy; monsoon rain darkens pavements and makes leaves shine. Many people wear a longyi with a shirt or blouse, though modern trousers are common too. “မင်္ဂလာပါ” (mingalaba) is a greeting; “ဦး” (U) and “ဒေါ်” (Daw) are respectful titles. Market voices mingle with bicycle bells and rain on metal roofs.

Namibia’s flag has a red diagonal band running from lower hoist to upper fly, edged in white; blue fills the upper hoist triangle and green the lower fly triangle. A gold sun with twelve triangular rays sits in the blue. Windhoek has low-rise streets, modern offices and the red-roofed Christuskirche; beyond the towns lie ochre dunes, gravel plains and sparse thorn trees. Atlantic fog often softens the light at Swakopmund, while inland sun casts hard shadows. People wear varied contemporary clothes suited to heat or cool mornings. Greetings differ by language: “hello” is common in English, while Oshiwambo speakers say “Wa uhala po” in the morning and may respectfully address elders as “Tate” or “Meme.” Wind scuffs sand across roads.

Nauru is a small Pacific island with a narrow coastal road, low houses, coconut palms and white surf breaking against reef. Inland, pale limestone pinnacles and exposed rock mark parts of the raised plateau. Its flag is dark blue with a thin horizontal yellow stripe across the middle and a white twelve-pointed star below the stripe near the hoist. Bright tropical light gives the sea sharp turquoise and deep-blue bands; rain clouds can arrive quickly. People wear everyday light clothing and often travel by car or scooter. Waves hiss over the reef, with engines audible along the road. Greetings include Nauruan “Ekamowir Omo” and English “hello.”

Nepal’s flag is a crimson double pennant, not a rectangle, edged in blue: a white crescent moon is in the upper section and a white sun in the lower section. Kathmandu has brick courtyards, carved wooden windows, temple roofs and crowded streets where motorcycles weave slowly around pedestrians. Beyond the valleys, terraced green slopes rise toward snow-covered Himalayan peaks. Monsoon rain darkens the brick; clear mornings reveal crisp mountain silhouettes. Clothing ranges from shirts and jeans to saris, kurta suruwal and daura suruwal. Hear horns, footsteps and market conversation. People greet one another with “नमस्ते” (namaste) and may address an older man as “दाइ” (dai) or woman as “दिदी” (didi).

The Netherlands has a flag of three equal horizontal stripes: red on top, white in the middle and blue below. Amsterdam’s narrow brick canal houses have tall windows and steep gables; bicycles pass over arched bridges beside moored boats. Elsewhere, flat fields, drainage canals, wind turbines and occasional historic windmills sit under broad, changeable skies. Rain leaves cobblestones reflective, while low sunlight stretches long shadows across the water. People wear practical everyday clothes, often with rain jackets while cycling. Bicycle bells, tram wheels and boat engines punctuate street noise. Common greetings are “hallo” and “goedemorgen”; polite forms of address include “meneer” and “mevrouw.”

New Zealand’s flag has a blue field, the Union Jack in the upper hoist corner, and four red five-pointed stars with white borders to the right. Auckland mixes glass towers, low-rise neighborhoods and a harbor dotted with sailing boats; beyond the cities are green hills, rugged coasts and, in the South Island, snow-capped mountains. Wind ripples long grass and boat rigging; coastal light shifts quickly as clouds pass. People wear varied everyday clothes, with jackets common in cooler or wet weather. Hear gulls, traffic and halyards tapping against masts. “Kia ora” is a widely used greeting; “hello” and the informal address “mate” are also heard.

Nicaragua’s flag has three equal horizontal stripes, blue, white and blue, with its coat of arms centered on the white stripe: a triangle containing five volcanoes, a rainbow and a red Phrygian cap, surrounded by the words “REPUBLICA DE NICARAGUA AMERICA CENTRAL.” In Granada, colorful plaster façades and clay-tile roofs line streets beneath church towers; elsewhere, volcanoes rise near broad lakes and Pacific beaches. Warm sunlight casts hard midday shadows, while tropical rain drums on metal roofs. People wear light everyday clothing. Markets sound with voices, motorcycle engines and vendors calling. Greetings include “hola” and “buenos días”; “don” or “doña” can precede a person’s name respectfully.

Niger’s flag has three equal horizontal stripes—orange, white and green—with an orange circle centered in the white stripe. In Niamey, the Niger River passes sandy banks, bridges, markets and low concrete buildings. Farther north, Sahel scrub gives way to pale desert ground and dunes. Dry-season light can be hazy with dust; the rainy season briefly greens open land. Clothing includes everyday shirts and trousers as well as flowing robes and head coverings suited to sun and dust. Hear market bargaining, passing motorcycles and wind moving loose sand. French greetings include “bonjour” and the respectful “monsieur” or “madame”; Hausa speakers may greet someone with “sannu.”

Nigeria’s flag consists of three equal vertical stripes: green at the hoist, white in the center and green at the fly. Lagos has dense roads, bright shop signs, concrete towers and bridges crossing waterways; Abuja has broad avenues with Aso Rock rising behind parts of the city. Landscapes also range from humid southern vegetation to drier northern plains. Sunlight glints off car roofs after heavy rain. People wear varied modern clothing alongside agbada, kaftans and colorful patterned garments. Hear traffic horns, market calls and music from shops. Greetings vary by language: English “good morning,” Hausa “sannu,” Yoruba “ẹ káàárọ̀” and Igbo “ndewo”; “sir” or “ma” can be respectful forms of address.

North Korea’s flag has a wide red horizontal center band, narrow white bands above and below it, and blue bands along the top and bottom. A white disk near the hoist in the red band contains a red five-pointed star. Pyongyang has broad avenues, apartment blocks, monuments and the Juche Tower beside the Taedong River; outside the capital are fields, wooded hills and mountains. Winter light can be pale and cold, while summers are green and humid. People wear shirts, trousers, dresses and jackets according to season and setting. Hear footsteps on wide pavements, buses and river wind. A formal greeting is “안녕하십니까” (annyeonghasimnikka); “선생님” (seonsaengnim) is a respectful form of address.

North Macedonia’s flag is red with a central yellow sun and eight broad yellow rays reaching the edges. Skopje has pale stone buildings beside the Vardar River, an old stone bridge, mosque minarets, market lanes and modern apartment blocks. Beyond it, mountains frame lakes, villages and winding roads. Summers bring strong sun and dry-looking hillsides; winter can bring snow and low cloud. People commonly wear contemporary jackets, jeans and dresses, with clothing varying by community and occasion. Footsteps echo on stone lanes; cafés and traffic fill busier streets. People greet each other with “Здраво” or “Добар ден” and may politely address someone as “господине” or “госпоѓо”.

Norway’s flag is red with a dark blue Nordic cross outlined in white; the vertical arm sits closer to the hoist. Oslo’s waterfront has glass buildings, ferries and the sloping white Opera House, while Bergen has closely packed, colourful timber facades. Outside the cities are steep fjords, spruce forests, bare mountain rock and narrow roads. Coastal weather changes quickly, shifting from clear light to rain and mist; northern winter daylight can be brief. People wear practical coats and waterproof layers, often with wool underneath. Ferry engines hum and gulls call over the water. “Hei” and “God dag” are greetings; people usually use given names and the informal “du”.

Oman’s flag has horizontal white, red and green bands from top to bottom, crossed at the hoist by a vertical red band bearing a white khanjar and crossed swords near its top. Muscat’s low white buildings, arches and minarets sit between rocky Hajar slopes and blue sea. Elsewhere, date palms line wadis and dunes meet open desert. Bright sun makes walls glare; heat haze softens distant ridges. Many men wear light dishdashas and embroidered kumma caps, while women’s clothing ranges from abayas and scarves to other contemporary dress. Market voices, seabirds and passing cars mingle. “السلام عليكم” is a common greeting, answered “وعليكم السلام”; “أستاذ” is a polite form of address.

Pakistan’s flag has a white vertical stripe at the hoist and a dark green field bearing a white crescent and five-pointed star. Karachi has dense roads and coastal air; Lahore has brick buildings and grand Mughal-era domes; Islamabad’s broad avenues face green hills. Farther north, steep mountains hold snow. City light can be dusty and warm, with monsoon rain darkening roads in season. People wear shalwar kameez as well as shirts, trousers and other contemporary clothes. Buses rumble, horns sound and tea glasses clink at roadside stalls. In Urdu, people say “السلام علیکم,” reply “وعلیکم السلام,” and may address someone respectfully as “جناب”.

Palau’s flag is light blue with a large yellow disc set slightly toward the hoist. Around Koror, low concrete buildings and bridges connect green islands above clear turquoise water. Offshore Rock Islands rise as rounded, tree-covered limestone shapes with undercut edges; reefs show through shallow lagoons. Tropical sun casts sharp shadows between sudden rain showers. People commonly wear light shirts, shorts, dresses and sandals, with more formal clothing for ceremonies. Small boats lift and settle on waves, outboard motors buzz, and wind rustles palms. In Palauan, “Alii” is a greeting; elders may be addressed respectfully as “rubak” or “mechas”.

Palestine’s flag has horizontal black, white and green bands from top to bottom, with a red triangle extending from the hoist. Jerusalem’s Old City has pale limestone walls and the gold Dome of the Rock; Bethlehem and Ramallah have steep streets and stone buildings, while Gaza lies along the Mediterranean coast. Olive trees, terraced hills and dry summer light shape much of the landscape; winters can be cool and rainy. People wear contemporary clothes, with headscarves common among some women and embroidered thobes seen on special occasions. Street vendors, traffic, church bells or calls to prayer sound in different places. “السلام عليكم” and “مرحبا” are greetings; “أستاذ” and “أستاذة” are polite addresses.
