Panama’s flag has four quarters: white with a blue star at upper left, solid red at upper right, solid blue at lower left, and white with a red star at lower right. Panama City’s glass towers rise beside the bay, while Casco Viejo has balconies, pastel stucco and narrow streets. At the canal, huge ships move slowly through concrete locks as water rises or drains around them. Tropical forest stays lush through heavy seasonal rain; humid sunlight flashes off wet pavement. People wear light contemporary clothes, with office shirts and dresses in business districts. Traffic hums, birds call and ship horns carry over water. “Buenos días” is polite; “¿Qué xopá?” is informal, with “señor” or “señora” used respectfully.

Papua New Guinea’s flag is divided diagonally into a red upper-right triangle with a yellow bird-of-paradise silhouette and a black lower-left triangle with five white Southern Cross stars. Port Moresby spreads across dry-looking coastal hills with concrete buildings and busy roads; elsewhere, rainforest, mangroves and cloud-covered highland ridges dominate. Tropical light is intense, and rain can fall suddenly. Everyday clothing includes shirts, skirts and trousers; woven bilum bags are widely carried, while elaborate dress belongs to particular ceremonies and communities. Market chatter, birds and passing vehicles create distinct layers of sound. In widely used Tok Pisin, “Moning” is a greeting, “Yu orait?” asks how someone is, and “brata” or “sista” can be friendly forms of address.

Paraguay’s flag has horizontal red, white and blue stripes. Unusually, its faces differ: the front shows a star inside a wreath on the white stripe; the reverse shows a lion beside a liberty cap. In Asunción, low-rise stucco buildings, shaded plazas and modern towers sit beside broad roads carrying buses and motorcycles. Beyond the capital, reddish soil, pasture and palms stretch under bright, humid skies; summer rain darkens pavement quickly. People wear light shirts, jeans and sandals, with tereré flasks common in the heat. Spanish greetings include “Hola” and “Buen día, señora”; in Guaraní, “Mba’éichapa?” asks how someone is.

Peru’s flag has three equal vertical bands, red, white and red. The plain version is common; the state version bears a central shield showing a vicuña, a cinchona tree and a cornucopia. Coastal Lima has pale, often overcast light, dense traffic, concrete apartments and colonial balconies. Inland, steep Andean slopes frame stone streets and terraced fields; the Amazon region is green and humid. Clothing ranges from office wear and jeans to woven Andean hats and layered skirts in some communities. Footsteps click on stone, while buses rumble through narrow streets. People greet one another with “Buenos días, señor” or “señora”; Quechua speakers may say “Rimaykullayki.”

The Philippine flag has a white triangle at the hoist, a blue upper band and red lower band. A golden sun with eight rays sits in the triangle, with one golden star at each corner. Manila’s skyline mixes glass towers, concrete buildings, jeepneys and crowded roadside shops; elsewhere, palms, rice fields, volcanic hills and bright coastal water shape the view. Tropical light is strong, and sudden rain drums on metal roofs and sends water across streets. People commonly wear T-shirts, light blouses and sandals. “Kumusta po?” is a polite greeting; “Ate” and “Kuya” are familiar respectful ways to address an older woman or man.

Poland’s flag consists of two equal horizontal bands, white above red, without an emblem. Warsaw pairs glass office towers with reconstructed older streets, while many towns have painted façades around paved market squares. Trams ring over tracks; shoes scrape on icy pavements in winter. Flat fields and forests occupy much of the countryside, with mountains along the south and a Baltic coast to the north. Light shifts from short, grey winter days to long, warm summer evenings. People wear coats, scarves and boots in cold months and lighter everyday clothes in summer. “Dzień dobry” is a polite hello; strangers are addressed as “pan” or “pani.”

Portugal’s flag is green on the hoist-side two-fifths and red on the remaining three-fifths. Centered over their boundary is a yellow armillary sphere bearing a white shield with five smaller blue shields and a red border with seven yellow castles. Lisbon rises over hills of pale buildings, tiled façades and narrow streets where yellow trams squeal around bends. Beyond the cities are Atlantic beaches, cork-oak country and vineyards. Coastal light can be bright and breezy; winters are wetter. People commonly wear jeans, shirts and light jackets. “Bom dia” greets someone in the morning; “senhor” and “senhora” are polite forms of address.

Romania’s flag has three equal vertical bands: blue at the hoist, then yellow and red, with no emblem. Bucharest combines broad boulevards, apartment blocks, older ornate façades and the vast Palace of the Parliament. In Transylvanian towns, pitched roofs and pastel buildings line cobbled squares; beyond them lie Carpathian forests, farms and mountain roads. Traffic hums in cities, while church bells carry across some squares. Winters can bring snow and flat grey light; summers are warm and sunny. People dress in contemporary coats, jeans or office clothes, with traditional embroidered garments appearing at festivals. “Bună ziua” is a polite greeting; address someone as “domnule” or “doamnă.”

Rwanda’s flag has a blue upper half, then equal yellow and green quarters beneath it, with a golden sun of 24 rays near the upper fly. Kigali spreads across green hills: paved roads curve past modern mid-rise buildings, tidy shops and planted verges. Outside the city, terraced slopes, banana plants and tea fields appear through mist, especially in the cooler highlands. Motorcycles buzz uphill, and rain can patter heavily before sunlight returns. People wear contemporary shirts, dresses, trousers and jackets; colourful patterned fabrics also appear. In Kinyarwanda, “Muraho” means hello and “Mwaramutse” is a morning greeting; people may politely address someone as “Bwana” or “Madamu.”

The flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis is green at the upper hoist and red at the lower fly, divided by a rising diagonal black band with narrow yellow borders and two white stars. Basseterre has low, colourful buildings, verandas and streets leading toward a busy waterfront. Volcanic slopes rise behind settlements; Nevis has a prominent cloud-touched peak, with beaches and palms around its coast. Sunlight is sharp, sea air is humid, and rain showers briefly rattle roofs. People commonly wear light shirts, dresses, shorts and sandals. English greetings include “Good morning, sir” or “ma’am”; in casual local speech, “Wha gwan?” asks what is happening.

Saint Lucia’s flag is a sky-blue field with a tall central black triangle edged in white and a smaller golden-yellow triangle rising in front of it. The twin, steep-sided Pitons rise beside Soufrière above dark volcanic shorelines and green forest; Castries has a sheltered harbor, low-rise shops, and busy minibus stops. Strong tropical sun casts sharp shadows before passing showers soften the view. People wear lightweight shirts, dresses, and sandals, with brighter formal clothes for celebrations. Waves slap against fishing boats, while markets carry conversation and traffic noise. Greetings include “Hello” and Kwéyòl “Bonjou”; adults may be addressed as “Misyé” or “Madam.”

The flag has vertical blue, yellow, and green bands, with the middle yellow band twice as wide and three green diamonds arranged in a V at its center. On Saint Vincent, Kingstown’s low buildings and arched shopfronts sit beneath steep green hills; smaller Grenadine islands have pale beaches, clear shallows, and anchorages dotted with boats. Tropical light glints off water, and brief rain darkens roads quickly. Ferries rock gently at their moorings; engines, seabirds, and market voices fill the waterfront. People commonly wear breathable everyday clothes and sandals. “Good morning” or “Mornin’” opens a greeting; “Miss,” “Mister,” or “Sir” addresses someone politely.

Samoa’s flag is red with a blue rectangle in the upper hoist corner bearing five white, five-pointed Southern Cross stars. Around Apia, low buildings, a clock tower, markets, and waterfront roads sit between the sea and lush volcanic slopes. Villages include open-sided fale with broad roofs supported by posts; palms and breadfruit trees edge the roads. Humid daylight is bright, and tropical downpours drum loudly on roofs. Buses rattle past, while waves break against reef shallows. Clothing includes shirts, dresses, and patterned lavalava; formal occasions may call for finer woven garments. People greet each other with “Talofa” or “Talofa lava” and may respectfully address someone as “susuga.”

San Marino’s flag has equal horizontal white and pale-blue bands, with the national coat of arms centered: three white towers on green peaks, a crown above, a wreath around them, and a ribbon reading “LIBERTAS” below. Stone towers crown Mount Titano above compact streets, pale masonry buildings, and steep lanes with broad views across the surrounding hills. In summer, sunlight picks out the rough stone; cooler months bring mist and jackets. Footsteps and conversation echo along narrow passages, while cars remain on wider roads. People wear contemporary Italian-style everyday clothing. They greet with “Buongiorno” or “Salve” and politely address adults as “signore” or “signora.”

The flag of São Tomé and Príncipe has narrow green stripes above and below a wider yellow stripe, two black five-pointed stars across the yellow, and a red triangle extending from the hoist. São Tomé’s waterfront has low pastel buildings, palms, and a harbor; inland, dense rainforest climbs volcanic hills, with the narrow rock spire Pico Cão Grande rising sharply above the trees. Warm, humid light alternates with heavy rain. Waves, insects, and motorbikes are common sounds, and wet leaves shine after showers. People wear light shirts, dresses, and sandals. Portuguese greetings include “Bom dia” and “Boa tarde”; polite forms of address are “senhor” and “senhora.”

Senegal’s flag has three equal vertical bands of green, yellow, and red, with a green five-pointed star centered on the yellow band. Dakar mixes concrete mid-rise buildings, busy roadside stalls, and ocean-facing roads; elsewhere, sandy Sahel landscapes give way to greener riverbanks and coastal mangroves. Sunlight is strong, with dusty haze at times, especially inland. Colorful buses brake and rattle, market vendors call out, and Atlantic surf breaks along the coast. Clothing ranges from T-shirts and trousers to flowing boubous and headwraps. In Wolof, people greet with “Nanga def?”; “As-salaam maalekum” is also common. In French, respectful address includes “monsieur” and “madame.”

Serbia’s flag has equal horizontal red, blue, and white bands, with a crowned coat of arms toward the hoist: a white double-headed eagle bearing a smaller red shield with a white cross and four firesteels. Belgrade has layered stone fortifications above the Sava and Danube, broad streets, apartment blocks, and café terraces. Beyond the cities are farmland, wooded hills, and mountains. Summer sun can be intense; winter brings grey skies and occasional snow. Trams squeal around bends, and conversation carries from cafés. People wear contemporary European clothing, adding heavy coats in winter. “Dobar dan” and “Zdravo” are common greetings; polite address includes “gospodine” and “gospođo.”

The Seychelles flag fans out from the lower hoist corner in five broad diagonal bands: blue, yellow, red, white, and green, in that order from top to bottom. On Mahé, Victoria’s low buildings and busy streets lie between a harbor and densely green hills. Elsewhere, smooth granite boulders frame pale beaches, with palms leaning above clear turquoise shallows. Humid sunlight flashes on the sea, and short showers leave pavement glossy. Fishing boats bob and knock softly against jetties; waves and tropical birds are easy to hear. People wear light shirts, dresses, and sandals. In Seychellois Creole, greetings include “Bonzour” and “Bonswar”; respectful address includes “Msye” and “Madanm.”

Sierra Leone’s flag has three equal horizontal bands: green, white and blue from top to bottom. In Freetown, tightly packed concrete buildings and corrugated roofs climb steep green hills above the Atlantic; streets carry yellow taxis and crowded minibuses called poda-podas. Inland, laterite-red roads cut through forest and farmland. Humid daylight can turn abruptly grey before heavy rain, which drums on metal roofs and sends water rushing along roadside drains. People wear T-shirts, office clothes, patterned fabrics and headwraps. In Krio, a greeting is “Aw di bodi?” (“How are you?”); “broda” and “sista” are familiar forms of address.

Singapore’s flag is red above white in equal horizontal halves, with a white crescent and five white stars arranged in a circle at the upper hoist. Marina Bay has glass towers, three Marina Bay Sands towers joined by a boat-shaped roof, and the branching steel Supertrees. Elsewhere, painted shophouses stand beside uniform high-rise housing blocks and sheltered walkways. Tropical light is bright and humid; sudden rain hisses on pavement while buses, trains and food-court kitchens add a steady hum. Clothing ranges from office wear to casual shorts and religious dress. Greetings include “Hello,” Malay “Selamat pagi,” and Mandarin “你好”; older people may be addressed as “uncle” or “auntie.”

Slovakia’s flag has equal white, blue and red horizontal bands, with a red shield near the hoist bearing a white double cross above three blue hills. Bratislava’s pale hilltop castle overlooks the Danube, tram lines, stone squares and rows of stucco buildings; beyond the cities are wooded valleys, villages and the jagged High Tatras. Summer light is clear, while winter brings low sun, frost and snow. Tram wheels squeal around bends, and footsteps click on old paving. People wear contemporary European clothes, with coats and boots in winter. “Dobrý deň” is a polite greeting; “pán” and “pani” precede names in formal address.

Slovenia’s flag has equal white, blue and red horizontal bands. Near the upper hoist is a shield showing white Mount Triglav, two blue wavy lines beneath it and three six-pointed gold stars above. Ljubljana has a river crossed by compact stone bridges, pastel facades, a hilltop castle and leafy streets. Farther northwest, steep limestone peaks rise above green valleys and Lake Bled. Soft morning mist often clears to crisp daylight; church bells, bicycle tyres and river water are common sounds. People generally wear casual European clothing, with hiking layers in the mountains. “Dober dan” is a polite greeting; “gospod” and “gospa” are formal forms of address.

The Solomon Islands flag is divided diagonally by a narrow yellow stripe running from lower hoist to upper fly: blue with five white stars at the upper hoist, green at the lower fly. In Honiara, low concrete shops and houses with broad roofs sit between forested hills and the sea. Elsewhere, villages line beaches beside palms, mangroves and clear reef water. Humid sun makes metal roofs glint; rain arrives in dense, noisy sheets. Outboard motors buzz across bays, while small boats rock and leave spreading wakes. People wear light shirts, skirts and dresses. In Solomon Islands Pijin, “Halo, hao nao?” is a greeting; “brata” and “sista” are familiar forms of address.

Somalia’s flag is plain light blue with one white five-pointed star centered on it. Mogadishu faces the Indian Ocean: pale concrete streets, older coral-stone buildings, mosques, markets and bright sandy shore appear under strong coastal light. Inland, dry plains carry sparse acacia trees beneath a wide sky. Sea wind flutters loose fabric and market awnings; traffic, conversation and surf overlap in the soundscape. Clothing includes shirts and trousers, long dresses, colourful wraps, headscarves and traditional macawis. Greetings include Somali “Iska warran?” (“How are you?”) and “Salaan.” “Walaal,” meaning sibling, is a warm, respectful way to address someone.

South Africa’s flag has red above blue, separated by a green Y edged in white; at the hoist, a black triangle has a yellow border. Cape Town’s flat-topped Table Mountain rises behind streets and the harbour, while Johannesburg has a denser skyline of towers and broad roads. Landscapes range from grassy veld to rocky coast and dry interior. Sunlight is often sharp; wind rattles trees and surf breaks loudly along beaches. People wear varied urban fashions, work clothes and garments reflecting many communities. Greetings vary by language: isiZulu “Sawubona,” isiXhosa “Molo,” and Afrikaans “Goeie dag.” “Sisi” and “bhuti” are familiar forms of address in some settings.

South Korea’s white flag carries a central red-over-blue taegeuk circle and four black trigrams: three solid bars at upper left, broken-solid-broken at upper right, solid-broken-solid at lower left, and three broken bars at lower right. Seoul’s Han River passes dense apartment towers, glass offices and bridges; Gyeongbokgung’s tiled roofs stand beneath wooded mountains. Streets mix bright shop signs, narrow restaurants and busy crossings. Seasons change visibly, from humid green summers to crisp autumns and cold winters. Subway chimes, traffic and conversation fill the air. People wear contemporary clothes, with hanbok sometimes worn for celebrations. “안녕하세요” is a polite greeting; “선생님” is a respectful form of address.

South Sudan’s flag has horizontal black, red, and green bands separated by narrow white stripes, with a blue triangle at the hoist holding a yellow five-pointed star. In Juba, low concrete buildings, corrugated roofs, roadside stalls, and dusty streets sit near the broad White Nile. Beyond town, flat savanna turns intensely green during the rains; puddles splash under tires, while dry-season wind lifts fine dust. Sunlight is strong and warm, with hazy afternoons. People wear shirts and trousers, patterned dresses, or tailored traditional clothing. English and Juba Arabic are heard; a greeting may be “Keif halak?” followed by “Kwayyis.”

Sri Lanka’s flag has a yellow border around two vertical hoist panels, green then orange, and a maroon field bearing a yellow lion holding a sword, with four yellow bo leaves in the corners. Colombo mixes glass towers and the narrow Lotus Tower with older buildings, crowded markets, buses, and three-wheel tuk-tuks that buzz and rattle through traffic. Inland, tea-covered slopes rise into mist; along the coast, palms bend in humid sea breezes. Monsoon rain drums sharply on metal roofs. People wear shirts and trousers, dresses, saris, or sarongs. Sinhala speakers greet with “Ayubowan”; Tamil speakers say “Vanakkam.”

Sudan’s flag has three equal horizontal bands, red, white, and black, with a green triangle extending from the hoist. Khartoum lies where the Blue and White Niles meet: broad riverbanks, bridges, low tan buildings, shaded courtyards, and busy streets stretch beneath a pale, often dusty sky. Outside irrigated land, dry plains carry sparse acacia trees; heat shimmers above asphalt and wind brushes sand against walls. Markets sound with conversation, car horns, and metal shutters. Clothing includes shirts and trousers, white jalabiyas, and colorful wrapped tobes. People commonly say “السلام عليكم” (as-salamu alaykum) and address someone respectfully as “يا أستاذ” (ya ustaz).

Suriname’s flag has five horizontal bands, green, white, red, white, and green, in a 2:1:4:1:2 ratio, with a yellow five-pointed star centered on the red. Paramaribo’s streets feature white wooden colonial-era buildings with dark shutters and steep roofs, alongside concrete shops, mosques, temples, and the tall timber Saint Peter and Paul Cathedral. Riverfront air is humid; rain falls heavily, then sunlight glints on wet pavement. Dense rainforest and wide brown rivers cover much of the interior, alive with insects and birds. People wear everyday urban clothes or festive traditional dress. In Dutch, “Goedemorgen” means good morning; in Sranan Tongo, friends ask “Fa waka?”

Sweden’s rectangular blue flag carries a yellow Nordic cross whose vertical bar sits closer to the hoist. Stockholm spreads across islands: pale stone facades, ochre and rust-colored buildings in Gamla Stan, church spires, ferries, and clean-lined trams frame cold blue water. Elsewhere, dark conifer forests border lakes; far north, snow can blanket roads for months. Winter light stays low and silver, while summer evenings linger brightly. Footsteps crunch on snow, and trams hum over rails. People commonly wear practical coats and boots in winter, lighter casual clothes in summer. Greetings include “Hej” and “God morgon”; people usually address each other with “du” and a first name.

Switzerland’s flag is square and red, with a centered white cross of four equal arms that do not touch the edges. Cities show distinct streetscapes: Bern has sandstone arcades and the Zytglogge clock tower, while Zurich has trams, stone buildings, and a lakeshore. Beyond them, steep Alpine slopes rise above clear lakes, pasture, and timber chalets. Train wheels click through mountain curves; cowbells carry across quiet fields. Light is crisp at altitude, with snowy winters and green summers. Clothing is mostly contemporary and weather-conscious. Greetings vary by language: “Grüezi” in Swiss German, “Bonjour” in French-speaking areas, and “Buongiorno” in Italian-speaking areas.

Taiwan’s flag is red, with a blue canton at the upper hoist containing a white sun with twelve pointed rays. Taipei’s skyline is marked by the tiered Taipei 101 tower; below it, scooters stream past convenience stores, apartment blocks, night-market stalls, and temples with vividly painted, upturned roofs. Green mountains rise sharply beyond dense neighborhoods, while the east coast meets the Pacific along steep cliffs. Humid summer air softens distant views, and heavy rain hisses on pavement. People wear casual modern clothes and carry umbrellas against rain or sun. Mandarin greetings include “你好” (nǐ hǎo); a shopkeeper may be addressed as “老闆” (lǎobǎn).

Tajikistan’s flag has horizontal red, white, and green bands in a 2:3:2 ratio. A gold crown sits in the white band beneath an arc of seven gold five-pointed stars. Dushanbe has broad avenues, pale government buildings, fountains, tree-lined parks, and mountains visible beyond the city. Farther east, the Pamirs form high, rocky ridges above winding roads and cold rivers; tires crunch on gravel, and wind whistles through exposed passes. Summers can be bright and dry, while mountain winters bring deep snow. People wear contemporary clothes, sometimes with embroidered caps or patterned headscarves. In Tajik, “Салом” (salom) is a greeting; “ака” (aka) respectfully addresses an older man.

Tanzania’s flag has a green upper-hoist triangle and blue lower-fly triangle, separated by a black diagonal band edged in yellow, running from lower hoist to upper fly. Dar es Salaam has low and mid-rise buildings, crowded markets, palms and bright Indian Ocean light; inland, dry grasslands contrast with Kilimanjaro’s high, pale slopes. Streets carry buses, motorcycles and pedestrians in everyday shirts, dresses and colourful printed fabrics. A market scene moves with fluttering awnings and people stepping around produce crates, amid engines and conversation. In Swahili, people say “Habari?”; a younger person may greet an elder with “Shikamoo,” answered by “Marahaba.”

Thailand’s flag has five horizontal stripes: red, white, blue, white and red, with the central blue stripe twice as wide as each other stripe. Bangkok mixes glass towers, concrete shopfronts, elevated trains, temple roofs and slow riverboats. Beyond the capital are rice fields, limestone cliffs and tropical coasts. Warm, humid light reflects from wet pavement during rainy spells. Motorbikes thread through traffic with a rising engine buzz; market stalls hiss as food cooks. People wear ordinary contemporary clothes, with modest dress at temples. A common greeting is “Sawatdee khrap” from a man or “Sawatdee kha” from a woman, often with palms pressed together in a wai.

Timor-Leste’s flag is red, with a yellow triangle extending from the hoist toward the centre and a smaller black triangle over it; a white five-pointed star sits in the black triangle. Dili has low concrete buildings, roadside kiosks and a waterfront facing calm blue water, with steep green hills close behind. Outside town, narrow roads pass dry-season brown slopes and greener valleys. Harsh midday sun casts short shadows; rain darkens the roads and brings dripping eaves. People wear contemporary shirts, dresses and sandals, sometimes with woven tais cloth for ceremonies. In Tetum, “Bondia” greets someone in the morning; “Maun” and “Mana” are respectful forms of address.

Togo’s flag has five equal horizontal stripes alternating green, yellow, green, yellow and green. A red square at the upper hoist holds one white five-pointed star. In coastal Lomé, sandy roads and paved streets meet markets, low concrete buildings, motorcycles and the Atlantic shoreline. Farther north, the landscape includes drier savanna and scattered trees. Tropical daylight can be bright and hazy; rain leaves puddles that motorcycles steer around. People wear everyday shirts, trousers, dresses and printed fabrics. Traffic hums beneath market voices and ocean surf. French is widely used: “Bonjour, monsieur” and “Bonjour, madame” are polite greetings, alongside greetings in local languages.

Tonga’s flag is red with a white rectangle in the upper-hoist corner containing a centred red cross. Nukuʻalofa is low-rise: houses, churches, small shops and broad roadside trees sit near a flat waterfront. Across the islands are palms, pale beaches and shallow turquoise water; humid sunlight makes white walls and roofs look especially bright. Sea breezes move leaves and loose clothing, while waves lap against shore walls and boats knock softly at moorings. People wear contemporary clothes; a taʻovala, a woven waist mat, may be worn for formal occasions. “Mālō e lelei” is a greeting, and “Fēfē hake?” asks how someone is doing.

Trinidad and Tobago’s flag is red, crossed from upper hoist to lower fly by a black diagonal band with narrow white borders. Port of Spain has colourful low-rise buildings, commercial towers and streets backed by the Northern Range; Tobago has smaller settlements, green hills and beaches. Tropical sun produces sharp shadows, while heavy showers briefly blur hills and slick the roads. People wear varied contemporary clothes, with bright costumes appearing during Carnival rather than in everyday street scenes. Traffic, conversations and music carry through busy areas; palms rustle near the coast. Greetings include “Good morning, sir” or “Good morning, ma’am,” and the casual “Wha yuh say?”

Tunisia’s flag is red with a central white disk holding a red crescent and a red five-pointed star inside its opening. In Tunis, white walls, blue doors and narrow medina lanes contrast with broad streets and modern apartments. Elsewhere, olive groves, Mediterranean beaches, dry inland plains and southern desert towns change the backdrop. Strong summer sun makes pale walls glow; sea breezes stir awnings and café chairs scrape on stone. People wear varied contemporary clothes, and some women wear headscarves. Street conversation mixes with traffic and café sounds. In Tunisian Arabic, “Aslema” means hello and “Labes?” asks how someone is; “Si” can respectfully precede a man’s name.

Turkmenistan’s flag is green, with a vertical red band near the hoist bearing five stacked carpet-gul patterns and crossed olive branches below. A white crescent and five white stars sit in the upper fly. Ashgabat has wide avenues, pale marble-clad buildings and formal landscaped spaces; beyond it lie dry plains and the sandy Karakum Desert. In strong sunlight, white facades glare and building shadows fall sharply. Trees move in the wind while footsteps and passing cars sound across broad paved areas. People wear varied contemporary clothes; traditional embroidered garments and telpek fur hats appear on some occasions. In Turkmen, “Salam” means hello; “Ýagşymy?” asks how someone is, and “aga” respectfully addresses an older man.

Tuvalu’s light-blue flag has the Union Jack in the upper hoist corner and nine yellow five-pointed stars scattered across the fly. Low coral islands have pale sand, coconut palms, narrow roads and houses close to a turquoise lagoon; Funafuti has no high-rise skyline. Bright tropical sun casts short shadows, while clouds can bring sudden heavy rain. People wear light shirts, dresses and patterned lava-lava wraps. Bicycles and motorbikes roll slowly along the narrow land, with waves and palm fronds audible nearby. People greet one another with “Talofa” and commonly use given names when addressing neighbours.

Uganda’s flag has six horizontal stripes—black, yellow and red, repeated—with a white central disc showing a grey crowned crane with a red throat patch and one raised leg. Kampala spreads over green hills: low concrete and brick buildings, busy paved roads, roadside stalls and boda-boda motorcycles. Beyond the city are banana groves, red soil, lakes and lush vegetation. Equatorial daylight is strong, softened by cloud and frequent rain. People wear everyday shirts, trousers and dresses, alongside colourful gomesi dresses at celebrations. Traffic hums, motorcycles buzz and rain drums on roofs. In Luganda, people may greet with “Oli otya?” and address others respectfully as “ssebo” or “nnyabo.”

Ukraine’s flag is two equal horizontal bands, blue above yellow, without an emblem. Kyiv has broad streets, apartment blocks, golden-domed churches and wooded slopes above the Dnipro River; elsewhere, towns give way to fields, rivers and forests. Summer light can be warm and long, while winter brings low grey skies, frost and snow. People wear contemporary coats, jeans and trainers, with embroidered vyshyvanka shirts on special occasions. Trams rattle on rails, footsteps crunch on snow and church bells carry across open squares. A common greeting is “Добрий день” (dobryi den); polite forms of address include “пані” (pani) and “пане” (pane).

Uruguay’s flag has nine alternating white and blue horizontal stripes, starting with white, and a white upper-hoist canton bearing a golden Sun of May with a face and alternating straight and wavy rays. Montevideo’s waterfront has broad promenades, low- and mid-rise buildings, older stone façades and leafy streets. Inland, grassy plains roll gently beneath wide skies. Summer sun is bright; Atlantic wind moves hair, flags and waterside trees. People wear casual city clothes, and some carry a mate gourd and thermos. Buses rumble and seabirds call along the coast. Greetings include “Buen día”; friends may say “che,” while “señor” and “señora” are polite addresses.

Uzbekistan’s flag has horizontal blue, white and green bands, with thin red lines separating them; the upper-hoist blue band holds a white crescent and twelve white stars. Tashkent mixes wide tree-lined roads, modern buildings, apartment blocks and metro entrances. Samarkand and Bukhara have monumental turquoise-tiled domes, patterned brickwork and shaded courtyards. Dry summer sunlight creates sharp shadows; winters can be cold. People wear modern shirts, dresses and coats, with embroidered doppi skullcaps and patterned fabrics also visible. Market sellers call out above footsteps and traffic. A common greeting is “Assalomu alaykum”; “aka” and “opa” respectfully address older men and women.

Vanuatu’s flag has a red upper field and green lower field divided by a black, yellow-bordered Y shape. The black hoist triangle bears a yellow curved boar’s tusk around two crossed namele leaves. Port Vila has a low waterfront of shops, homes, roads and boats, backed by steep green hills. Across the islands, volcanic slopes, dense vegetation and beaches meet clear water. Humid tropical light turns soft under passing rain clouds. People wear light everyday clothes and colourful island dresses; woven mats appear at gatherings. Outboard motors buzz, rain patters on tin roofs and surf breaks ashore. In Bislama, greetings include “Halo” and “Gud moning”; familiar addresses include “brata” and “sista.”

Vatican City’s square flag has two equal vertical fields, yellow at the hoist and white at the fly. The white field carries crossed gold and silver keys tied with a red cord beneath a papal tiara. St. Peter’s Basilica rises behind an oval colonnaded square of pale stone; nearby are formal gardens, walls and compact historic buildings. Roman sunlight makes the stone glow, with long shadows in late afternoon. Visitors wear varied contemporary clothing, generally covering shoulders and knees inside sacred spaces; clergy may wear cassocks. Footsteps echo on paving and bells ring above crowd murmur. Italian greetings include “Buongiorno”; polite addresses include “signore,” “signora” and “Padre” for a priest.

Venezuela’s flag has equal horizontal yellow, blue and red bands, with eight white five-pointed stars in an arc across the blue. The official state flag also places the coat of arms at the yellow band’s hoist end. Caracas fills a mountain valley with dense apartment towers, busy roads and green slopes; elsewhere are Caribbean beaches, plains and highland scenery. Tropical daylight is strong, with sharp shadows between rain showers. People wear light shirts, jeans and dresses in the heat. Traffic, street vendors and music animate urban sidewalks, while coastal surf rolls ashore. Greetings include “Buenas”; friends may address each other as “chamo” or “chama,” and strangers as “señor” or “señora.”

Vietnam’s flag is red with one large yellow five-pointed star centered on it. Hanoi has narrow shophouses, lakes and tree-lined streets; Ho Chi Minh City has dense shopfronts, overhead cables and glass towers. Rice paddies reflect the sky, while limestone islands rise steeply from northern bays. Motorbikes flow around corners in close, steady streams, with engine hums and short horn beeps. Tropical light can turn abruptly from bright sun to heavy rain; roofs and roads glisten afterward. Dress ranges from T-shirts and helmets to áo dài for formal occasions. People say “Xin chào” and may address someone as “anh,” “chị,” or “em,” depending on age and relationship.

Yemen’s flag has three equal horizontal bands: red on top, white in the middle and black below, with no emblem. In Sana’a, tall earth-toned tower houses have white plaster patterns around their windows; elsewhere are coastal streets, stone mountain villages and terraced slopes. Dusty mountain light is sharp, while the Red Sea coast is hotter and more humid. Men may wear shirts and trousers or a thobe with a shawl; women’s clothing varies, including abayas and colourful local dresses. Footsteps sound on stone lanes, and market calls mingle with traffic. A hanging cloth moves lightly in a breeze. People greet each other with “السلام عليكم” and may say “يا أخي” or “يا أختي.”

Zambia’s flag is green, with three narrow vertical bands near the lower fly edge—red, black and orange from left to right—and an orange eagle above them. Lusaka has low-rise shops, markets, broad roads and scattered modern office blocks. Beyond the cities lie grassy plains, wooded areas and the broad Zambezi; at Victoria Falls, spray rises above the gorge and water roars continuously. Rainy-season clouds soften the light, while dry-season afternoons cast crisp shadows. People wear everyday shirts, dresses and trousers, sometimes with bright patterned fabrics. Buses brake with a hiss, and leaves shift in warm wind. In Nyanja, a greeting is “Muli bwanji?”; respectful forms of address include “Bambo” and “Amayi.”

Zimbabwe’s flag has seven horizontal stripes—green, yellow, red, black, red, yellow, green—and a white triangle at the hoist bearing a red star with a golden Zimbabwe Bird. Harare combines leafy avenues, markets, low-rise buildings and office towers. Outside the city are granite outcrops, open woodland and the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe; Victoria Falls sends drifting spray above a deep gorge. Dry-season sunlight gives the land crisp, warm tones. Clothing ranges from casual shirts and trousers to patterned dresses and formal wear. Minibuses rumble along roads, while wind rustles dry grass. In Shona, people say “Mhoro” or “Makadii?” and may respectfully address elders as “Baba” or “Amai.”
